notation.meaning: Weighted volume of a vertex set

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Symmetric two-sided conductance for weighted undirected graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The conductance of a nontrivial cut \(S\subsetneq V\) is
\[\phi(S):=\frac{w(\delta(S))}{\min\{\operatorname{vol}(S),\operatorname{vol}(V\setminus S)\}}.\]
The graph conductance is \(\phi(G):=\min_{\varnothing\ne S\subsetneq V}\phi(S)\), where cuts with a zero-volume side are excluded. By replacing a feasible side with its complement when necessary, the same objective is
\[\phi(G)=\min_{S:\ 0<\operatorname{vol}(S)\le\operatorname{vol}(V)/2}\frac{w(\delta(S))}{\operatorname{vol}(S)}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Conductance minimizes crossing-edge weight divided by the smaller weighted volume of the two sides.
knowledge_statements.title: Conductance Objectives

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The conductance objective and its equivalent smaller-volume form are mathematically consistent, but the record has no supporting citation or locator.

Minimum edge expansion of the graph

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cardinality-normalized edge expansion with weighted crossing edges.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The edge expansion of a nontrivial cut \(S\subsetneq V\) is
\[h(S):=\frac{w(\delta(S))}{\min\{|S|,|V\setminus S|\}}.\]
The edge-expansion objective for the graph is \(h(G):=\min_{\varnothing\ne S\subsetneq V}h(S)\). Choosing the smaller side of each bipartition yields the equivalent one-sided form
\[h(G)=\min_{S:\ 1\le |S|\le |V|/2}\frac{w(\delta(S))}{|S|}.\]
For unit weights this counts boundary edges per vertex on the smaller side.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Edge expansion minimizes crossing-edge weight divided by the cardinality of the smaller side.

children.title: Volume-versus-Cardinality Normalization
children.top_down_role: Regimes where volume and cardinality normalization produce differing behavior.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is an undirected weighted graph in which every vertex has the same positive weighted degree \(d\).
\(S\) is a nonempty proper subset of \(V\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\phi(S)=\frac{h(S)}{d},\qquad \phi(G)=\frac{h(G)}{d}.\]
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact comparison on weighted regular graphs; irregular graphs require degree bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If every vertex has weighted degree \(d>0\), then every vertex set satisfies \(\operatorname{vol}(S)=d|S|\). Consequently, for every nontrivial cut,
\[\phi(S)=\frac{w(\delta(S))}{d\min\{|S|,|V\setminus S|\}}=\frac{h(S)}{d}.\]
Taking the minimum over cuts gives \(\phi(G)=h(G)/d\). Hence volume and cardinality normalization select exactly the same minimizing cuts on a weighted \(d\)-regular graph, although their objective values differ by the fixed factor \(d\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a weighted regular graph, conductance equals edge expansion divided by the common degree, so both normalizations have the same optimal cuts.
knowledge_statements.title: Volume-versus-Cardinality Normalization

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Uniform sparsest cut and comparison with edge expansion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines uniform sparsity and gives its pointwise factor-two relationship with edge expansion in unweighted graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\) with edge costs \(c_e\ge 0\), the uniform sparsity of a nontrivial cut \(S\subsetneq V\) is \[\rho(S)=\frac{\sum_{e\in\delta(S)}c_e}{|S|\,|V\setminus S|}.\] This is the sparsest-cut objective when every distinct vertex pair has unit demand. notation.meaning: Total pair demand separated by S

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Undirected capacitated graph with arbitrary symmetric pair demands.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a cut \((S,V\setminus S)\), let its separated demand be
\[D(S):=\sum_{u\in S,\,v\in V\setminus S}d_{uv}.\]
Whenever \(D(S)>0\), the cut sparsity is \(c(\delta(S))/D(S)\). The nonuniform sparsest-cut value is
\[\Phi(c,d):=\min_{S\subseteq V:\ D(S)>0}\frac{c(\delta(S))}{D(S)}.\]
Uniform sparsest cut is the special case \(d_{uv}=1\) for all distinct pairs, subject to the chosen global normalization convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nonuniform sparsest cut minimizes crossing capacity divided by the total prescribed pair demand separated by the cut.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Nonuniform sparsest-cut objective and multiway extension
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines demand-normalized sparsity for two-way cuts and for edge deletions inducing multiple connected components.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let G=(V,E) be an undirected graph with c(e)>0 for e\in E and terminal pairs (s_i,t_i), i=1,\ldots,k, having demands d(i)>0. For S\subseteq V, let \delta(S)=\{(u,v)\in E:u\in S,\ v\notin S\} and I(S)=\{i:|S\cap\{s_i,t_i\}|=1\}. The sparsity ratio is \rho(S)=\frac{\sum_{e\in\delta(S)}c(e)}{\sum_{i\in I(S)}d(i)}, and the sparsest-cut problem minimizes \rho(S). If deleting F\subseteq E produces connected-component partition \mathcal S=\{S_1,\ldots,S_c\}, with I(\mathcal S)=\{i:s_i\in S_j,\ t_i\in S_\ell,\ j\ne\ell\}, then \rho(\mathcal S)=\frac{\sum_{e\in F}c(e)}{\sum_{i\in I(\mathcal S)}d(i)}.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cut's sparsity is its crossing-edge cost divided by the terminal demand it separates, and the sparsest-cut problem minimizes this ratio. For an edge deletion producing several components, the analogous ratio uses the deleted-edge cost and all demand separated between components.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \rho(S)=\frac{\sum_{e\in\delta(S)}c(e)}{\sum_{i\in I(S)}d(i)},\qquad \rho(\mathcal S)=\frac{\sum_{e\in F}c(e)}{\sum_{i\in I(\mathcal S)}d(i)}

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\lambda^*\) be the largest scalar \(\lambda\ge0\) for which every pair demand \(d_{uv}\) can be routed simultaneously at amount \(\lambda d_{uv}\) without exceeding any edge capacity. knowledge_statements.scope_note: Metric-LP and Gram-matrix SDP relaxations for weighted correlation clustering on a complete signed graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(V\) be finite, let \(E^+\mathbin{\dot\cup}E^-=\binom{V}{2}\), and let \(w_{ij}\ge 0\). The metric relaxation minimizes \[\sum_{ij\in E^+}w_{ij}d_{ij}+\sum_{ij\in E^-}w_{ij}(1-d_{ij})\] subject to \(d_{ii}=0\), \(0\le d_{ij}\le 1\), and \(d_{ij}\le d_{ik}+d_{kj}\) for all \(i,j,k\in V\). A compatible vector SDP introduces a Gram matrix \(X\succeq0\) satisfying \(X_{ii}=1\), \(0\le X_{ij}\le1\), and \(d_{ij}=1-X_{ij}\), together with the metric inequalities on \(d\). Every partition is feasible by assigning one orthonormal unit vector to each block, so that \(X_{ij}=1\) within blocks and \(X_{ij}=0\) between blocks. Consequently, both relaxations lower-bound the minimum disagreement objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The metric LP optimizes fractional separation distances. A compatible SDP represents same-block indicators by a positive-semidefinite Gram matrix; assigning orthonormal vectors to distinct blocks embeds every clustering, so both relaxations lower-bound minimum disagreement.

knowledge_statements.title: Resolution-Limit Phenomena
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact merge boundary exposing the global-scale resolution limit of configuration-model modularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For disjoint blocks \(A,B\) in a partition, let \(e(A,B)\) be their total connecting edge weight and \(\operatorname{vol}(A)=\sum_{i\in A}d_i\). Under Newman–Girvan modularity, replacing \(A,B\) by \(A\cup B\) changes the objective by \[\Delta Q=\frac{e(A,B)}{m}-\frac{\operatorname{vol}(A)\operatorname{vol}(B)}{2m^2}.\] Thus modularity strictly prefers merging whenever \(2m e(A,B)>\operatorname{vol}(A)\operatorname{vol}(B)\). Because this threshold depends on the graph-wide quantity \(m\), enlarging remote parts of a graph can make two locally unchanged communities merge-optimal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Modularity merges adjacent blocks when their connecting weight exceeds a threshold depending on total graph weight; remote graph growth can therefore erase otherwise unchanged small communities.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is an undirected weighted graph with \(m>0\).
\(A\) and \(B\) are distinct blocks of the current partition.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(2m e(A,B)>\operatorname{vol}(A)\operatorname{vol}(B)\Longrightarrow Q(\mathcal P\setminus\{A,B\}\cup\{A\cup B\})>Q(\mathcal P)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Null-Model Sensitivity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dependence of modularity values and maximizers on the chosen expected-edge matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix an undirected weighted adjacency matrix \(A\) with total weight \(m>0\). For a symmetric null-model matrix \(P\), define \(Q_P(\mathcal P)=(2m)^{-1}\sum_{ij}(A_{ij}-P_{ij})\mathbf 1\{i\sim_{\mathcal P}j\}\). If another null model is \(P'=P+\Delta P\), then every partition satisfies \[Q_{P'}(\mathcal P)-Q_P(\mathcal P)=-\frac{1}{2m}\sum_{i,j}\Delta P_{ij}\mathbf 1\{i\sim_{\mathcal P}j\}.\] Consequently, a nonconstant partition-dependent perturbation can reverse the ordering of two partitions and change the maximizing clustering even though \(A\) is unchanged.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Changing expected edge weights shifts each partition according to its within-block null-model mass, so the same observed graph can have a different modularity maximizer.
assumptions_latex: \(A,P,P'\) are symmetric matrices on the same finite vertex set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Q_{P'}(\mathcal P)-Q_P(\mathcal P)=-(2m)^{-1}\sum_{i\sim_{\mathcal P}j}\Delta P_{ij}\).

knowledge_statements.title: Scale-Selection Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pairwise merge regimes for resolution-parameter modularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\gamma>0\), define generalized modularity by \[Q_\gamma(\mathcal P)=\frac{1}{2m}\sum_{i,j}\left(A_{ij}-\gamma\frac{d_id_j}{2m}\right)\mathbf 1\{i\sim_{\mathcal P}j\}.\] For distinct blocks \(A,B\) with positive volumes, merging them has gain \(\Delta Q_\gamma=e(A,B)/m-\gamma\operatorname{vol}(A)\operatorname{vol}(B)/(2m^2)\). Hence the merge, tie, and separation regimes occur respectively at \(\gamma<\gamma_{AB}\), \(\gamma=\gamma_{AB}\), and \(\gamma>\gamma_{AB}\), where \(\gamma_{AB}=2m e(A,B)/(\operatorname{vol}(A)\operatorname{vol}(B))\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each pair of blocks has a critical resolution value: below it merging improves modularity, at it merging ties, and above it keeping the blocks separate is locally better.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{sign}(\Delta Q_\gamma)=\operatorname{sign}(\gamma_{AB}-\gamma)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Fixed-Count Graph Clustering
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimum weighted k-cut formulation with exactly k nonempty clusters.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E,w)\) be a finite undirected graph with \(w_e\ge0\), and let \(1\le k\le |V|\). A fixed-count graph clustering is a partition \(\mathcal P=(C_1,\ldots,C_k)\) of \(V\) into exactly \(k\) nonempty sets. In the minimum \(k\)-cut formulation its cost is \[\operatorname{cut}(\mathcal P)=\sum_{uv\in E}w_{uv}\mathbf 1\{u\text{ and }v\text{ lie in different }C_r\},\] and the optimization problem is to minimize this quantity over all such partitions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fixed-count clustering partitions the vertices into exactly k nonempty clusters and, in the minimum k-cut model, minimizes total weight crossing between clusters.

knowledge_statements.title: Hierarchical Cut Clustering
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rooted-tree hierarchical clustering with the standard weighted cut-based Dasgupta objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E,w)\) be a finite undirected similarity graph with \(w_{uv}\ge0\). A hierarchical clustering is a rooted tree \(T\) whose leaves are exactly \(V\). For leaves \(u,v\), let \(T_{uv}\) be the subtree rooted at their least common ancestor and let \(|T_{uv}|\) denote its number of leaves. The cut-based hierarchical cost is \[\operatorname{cost}_G(T)=\sum_{uv\in E}w_{uv}|T_{uv}|.\] Hierarchical cut clustering seeks a tree minimizing this cost; binary trees suffice under the usual refinement convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A hierarchy is a leaf-labeled rooted tree. Similar vertices are penalized by the size of the smallest cluster containing both, and the objective minimizes total weighted penalty.

knowledge_statements.title: Combinatorial-Laplacian Relaxation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rayleigh relaxation of unnormalized two-way spectral partitioning.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\) be a connected undirected weighted graph with adjacency matrix \(A\), degree matrix \(D\), combinatorial Laplacian \(L=D-A\), and all-ones vector \(\mathbf1\). Relaxing a discrete two-block indicator to a real vector gives \[\min\{x^{\mathsf T}Lx:x^{\mathsf T}x=1,\ x^{\mathsf T}\mathbf1=0\}=\lambda_2(L).\] Every minimizer is an eigenvector associated with the second-smallest eigenvalue. A discrete partition is subsequently obtained by thresholding such a vector; the relaxation value itself is the minimum Rayleigh quotient on \(\mathbf1^\perp\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Unnormalized spectral partitioning minimizes Laplacian energy over unit vectors orthogonal to constants. Its solutions are second-eigenvalue eigenvectors, which are then rounded into cuts.

knowledge_statements.title: Normalized-Laplacian Relaxations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Symmetric normalized-Laplacian relaxation for normalized-cut partitioning.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\) be a connected undirected weighted graph with positive degree matrix \(D\), Laplacian \(L=D-A\), and \(L_{\mathrm{sym}}=D^{-1/2}LD^{-1/2}\). knowledge_statements.title: Random-Walk Laplacian Relaxations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generalized-eigenvector form of the degree-normalized spectral relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\) be a connected undirected weighted graph with \(D\) positive diagonal and let \(L_{\mathrm{rw}}=D^{-1}L=I-D^{-1}A\). The degree-weighted relaxation is \[\min\{x^{\mathsf T}Lx:x^{\mathsf T}Dx=1,\ x^{\mathsf T}D\mathbf1=0\}=\lambda_2,\] where \(\lambda_2\) is the second-smallest generalized eigenvalue of \(Lx=\lambda Dx\), equivalently the second eigenvalue of \(L_{\mathrm{rw}}x=\lambda x\). Any minimizing generalized eigenvector can be thresholded to obtain a discrete partition.

knowledge_statements.title: Directed Cheeger Variants
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A directed conductance inequality obtained through stationary time-reversal symmetrization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\) be an irreducible finite Markov transition matrix with stationary distribution \(\pi\), and let \(P^*=\Pi^{-1}P^{\mathsf T}\Pi\) be its time reversal. Define \(M=(P+P^*)/2\) and \(\Phi(P)=\min_{0<\pi(S)\leq1/2}\sum_{i\in S,j\notin S}\pi_iP_{ij}/\pi(S)\). Stationarity implies \(\Phi(P)=\Phi(M)\). If \(\gamma=1-\lambda_2(M)\), then \[\frac{\gamma}{2}\leq\Phi(P)\leq\sqrt{2\gamma}.\] Hence the relevant real spectral gap is that of the additive reversiblization, not an ordering of the generally complex eigenvalues of \(P\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Directed stationary conductance equals that of the additive reversiblization and therefore obeys an ordinary Cheeger inequality for the reversiblized spectral gap.

knowledge_statements.title: Reversibility Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Why the reversible second-eigenvalue formulation does not transfer directly to directed chains.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the deterministic directed cycle on \(n\geq3\) states, let \(P_{i,i+1\bmod n}=1\). Its stationary distribution is uniform and its directed conductance is positive, of order \(n^{-1}\), but the eigenvalues of \(P\) are \(e^{2\pi i j/n}\), all on the unit circle. Consequently, there is no canonically ordered real second eigenvalue whose gap can satisfy the reversible Cheeger statement. The additive reversiblization \((P+P^*)/2\) instead has real gap \(1-\cos(2\pi/n)\), of order \(n^{-2}\), restoring the square-root conductance scaling.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A deterministic directed cycle has positive conductance but complex unit-modulus eigenvalues, so reversible Cheeger theory requires symmetrization or another nonreversible spectral surrogate.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) is the one-step deterministic transition matrix on the directed cycle.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The reversible formula cannot use a real ordered \(\lambda_2(P)\); additive reversiblization yields gap \(1-\cos(2\pi/n)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\) be a symmetric nonnegative adjacency matrix, with degrees defined by \(d_v=\sum_{j=1}^n A_{vj}\). knowledge_statements.title: Repeated-Eigenvalue Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Basis nonuniqueness and projector invariance for a repeated symmetric-Laplacian eigenvalue.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(L=L^{\mathsf T}\) and suppose an eigenvalue \(\lambda\) has multiplicity \(m>1\), with eigenspace \(E_\lambda\). If \(U\in\mathbb R^{n\times m}\) has orthonormal columns spanning \(E_\lambda\), then every other orthonormal eigenbasis matrix for that eigenspace is \(UQ\) for some orthogonal \(Q\in\mathbb R^{m\times m}\). Individual eigenvectors and their coordinate orderings are therefore not intrinsic. In contrast, the projector \(P_\lambda=UU^{\mathsf T}\), row distances \(\lVert U_{i,:}-U_{j,:}\rVert_2\), and row inner products are invariant under the basis replacement \(U\mapsto UQ\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A repeated eigenvalue determines an eigenspace, not unique eigenvectors; projectors and Euclidean relationships in the full eigenspace remain basis invariant.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every orthonormal basis change is \(U\mapsto UQ\), while \(UU^{\mathsf T}\) and all embedded row distances remain unchanged.

knowledge_statements.title: Basis-Selection Instability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Disconnected equal components show instability of rounding one vector from a repeated eigenspace.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\) be the disjoint union of two nonempty connected graphs \(G_1\) and \(G_2\). The normalized Laplacian has eigenvalue \(0\) with multiplicity two and eigenspace spanned by \(z_1=D^{1/2}\mathbf1_{V(G_1)}\) and \(z_2=D^{1/2}\mathbf1_{V(G_2)}\). Every nonzero combination \(a z_1+b z_2\) is a zero eigenvector. Consequently, a procedure selecting one numerical eigenvector and thresholding its coordinates can return different cuts after an orthogonal rotation within this eigenspace, even though the graph and invariant spectral projector are unchanged. The full two-dimensional embedding is stable up to rotation.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A spreading-metric relaxation is
\[\min \sum_{\{i,j\}\in E}w_{ij}d_{ij}\quad\text{subject to}\quad d_{ii}=0,\ d_{ij}=d_{ji},\ 0\le d_{ij}\le 1,\ d_{ij}\le d_{i\ell}+d_{\ell j},\ \sum_{j\in V}d_{ij}\ge |V|-b\quad(i,j,\ell\in V).\]
For any partition into blocks of size at most \(b\), setting \(d_{ij}=0\) within blocks and \(d_{ij}=1\) between blocks satisfies every constraint, and the objective equals the partition's cut weight. Consequently the relaxation optimum is a lower bound on the corresponding integral optimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A semimetric with triangle and spreading constraints relaxes balanced partitioning; every bounded-size partition gives a feasible zero-one metric of equal cut cost.
knowledge_statements.title: Spreading-Metric Relaxations

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The semimetric formulation is a suitable representation of cardinality-bounded spreading relaxation, but no inspectable source supports the exact constraint system.

assumptions_latex: \((V,d)\) is a finite metric space with \(|V|=n\ge 2\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A distribution over dominating tree metrics exists with expected pairwise stretch \(O(\log n)\).

notation.meaning: Shortest-path metric of a sampled weighted tree containing \(V\).

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: This is the standard probabilistic dominating-tree approximation theorem for finite metrics.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Probabilistic dominating-tree approximation; the universal constant is left unspecified.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
There is a probability distribution over weighted tree metrics \(d_T\) on trees whose vertex sets contain \(V\), and a universal constant \(C>0\), such that for every \(u,v\in V\),
\[d(u,v)\le d_T(u,v)\quad\text{almost surely},\qquad \mathbb E[d_T(u,v)]\le C\log n\,d(u,v).\]
Thus every finite metric admits a random noncontractive tree representation with expected pairwise distortion at most \(C\log n\). The expectation is taken over the sampled tree, separately for each fixed pair \((u,v)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every finite metric is dominated by a random tree metric whose expected stretch for each pair is logarithmic in the number of points.
knowledge_statements.title: Tree-Metric Approximations

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: This is the standard probabilistic dominating-tree theorem and theorem is the correct content kind, but its tree model and logarithmic guarantee require an authoritative theorem citation.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite \(\ell_1\) embeddings represented through the cut cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every nonempty proper \(S\subset V\), let \(\delta_S(u,v)=1\) when exactly one of \(u,v\) lies in \(S\), and let \(\delta_S(u,v)=0\) otherwise. A cut embedding of distortion \(D\ge1\) is a family \(\lambda_S\ge0\) such that
\[d(u,v)\le \sum_{\varnothing\ne S\subsetneq V}\lambda_S\delta_S(u,v)\le Dd(u,v)\qquad(u,v\in V).\]
The middle expression is an \(\ell_1\) metric, and every \(\ell_1\) metric on \(V\) has such an exact cut decomposition. Hence low-distortion cut embedding and low-distortion embedding into \(\ell_1\) are equivalent finite-metric formulations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite ell-one metrics are nonnegative sums of cut metrics, so low-distortion cut and ell-one embeddings are equivalent formulations.

If each vertex of $V$ is included in $S$ independently with probability $p=2^{-(t+1)}$, then $\Pr[(S\cap A=\varnothing)\land(S\cap B\ne\varnothing)]\ge \frac12(1-e^{-1/4})$.

children.title: Graph Coarsening Strategies
children.top_down_role: Graph-reduction strategies used to form multilevel hierarchies.

knowledge_statements.title: Graph Coarsening Strategies
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weighted aggregation coarsening with exact preservation of aggregate-respecting cut costs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Initialize \(G_0=G\). At level \(\ell\), choose a surjective aggregation map \(\pi_\ell:V_\ell\to V_{\ell+1}\) whose fibers are the selected aggregates. For distinct coarse vertices \(A,B\), set
\[w_{\ell+1}(A,B)=\sum_{\substack{\{u,v\}\in E_\ell\\ \pi_\ell(u)=A,\ \pi_\ell(v)=B}}w_\ell(u,v).\]
Discard self-loops. Stop when a prescribed vertex-count or contraction threshold is met, and output the graphs and aggregation maps. Every coarse partition lifts by assigning each fine vertex to its aggregate's block, and its lifted cut weight equals the coarse cut weight.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeatedly contract disjoint aggregates and sum interaggregate edge weights; every coarse partition then lifts with exactly the same cut cost.
assumptions_latex: \(G_0=(V_0,E_0,w_0)\) is a finite weighted undirected graph.
At each level, a contraction rule selects pairwise disjoint vertex aggregates.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The procedure produces a weighted hierarchy in which coarse cut weights equal the fine cut weights of lifted aggregate-respecting partitions.

notation.meaning: Map sending fine vertices to their aggregates.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Weighted aggregation by summing interaggregate edges is the standard contraction invariant.

children.title: Uncoarsening Schedules
children.top_down_role: Hierarchy-expansion regimes used during multilevel partition recovery.

assumptions_latex: A hierarchy \(G_0,\ldots,G_L\) with aggregation maps is given.
A feasible partition \(P_L\) has been computed on the coarsest graph.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The schedule returns a feasible fine-level partition and never increases cut cost when every accepted refinement move is nonincreasing.

notation.meaning: Aggregation map from level \(\ell\) to level \(\ell+1\).

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Projection followed by local refinement is the defining multilevel uncoarsening schedule.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Level-by-level projection with feasibility-preserving local refinement.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\ell=L-1,L-2,\ldots,0\), initialize \(P_\ell\) by assigning \(v\in V_\ell\) to the block containing \(\pi_\ell(v)\) in \(P_{\ell+1}\). Apply a specified local refinement oracle to \(P_\ell\), accepting only moves that preserve the balance constraints and do not increase cut weight; stop refinement when no accepted move remains or a level budget is exhausted. Output \(P_0\). Because projection preserves the coarse cut and every accepted move is nonincreasing, the cut-weight sequence across each projection-refinement stage is nonincreasing, while feasibility is maintained at every level.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Project the coarse partition down one level at a time and apply feasible nonincreasing local moves, yielding a no-worse fine partition.
knowledge_statements.title: Uncoarsening Schedules

children.title: Hierarchy-Quality Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Partition-quality effects of coarsening choices and hierarchy depth.

knowledge_statements.title: Hierarchy-Quality Tradeoffs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact search-space tradeoff for contraction-based minimization, independent of a particular coarsening heuristic.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mathcal F\) be the feasible fine-level partitions and let \(\mathcal F_\pi=\{P\in\mathcal F:P\text{ is constant on every aggregate of }\pi\}\). Then \(\mathcal F_\pi\subseteq\mathcal F\), and exact preservation of aggregate-respecting cut costs yields
\[\min_{P\in\mathcal F}\operatorname{cut}(P)\le \min_{P\in\mathcal F_\pi}\operatorname{cut}(P).\]
Merging additional aggregates can only shrink \(\mathcal F_\pi\), so the restricted optimum is nondecreasing while the number of coarse vertices is nonincreasing. Subsequent uncoarsening refinement may recover partitions excluded from the coarse search space.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: More contraction makes coarse problems smaller but restricts admissible partitions, so the exact restricted optimum can only worsen for cut minimization.
assumptions_latex: Each coarse vertex represents an indivisible aggregate of original vertices.
Cut weight is minimized over partitions satisfying fixed feasibility constraints.
Cut costs of aggregate-respecting partitions are preserved by contraction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Coarsening restricts the feasible search space, so its optimum cannot improve upon the unrestricted fine optimum, although it reduces instance size.

notation.meaning: Feasible partitions of the original graph.
Feasible original partitions constant on every aggregate.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: The quality ordering follows from inclusion of the aggregate-respecting feasible set.

children.title: Kernighan–Lin Refinement
children.top_down_role: Pair-exchange refinement regimes for graph partitions.

knowledge_statements.title: Kernighan–Lin Refinement
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical weighted, exactly balanced two-way pair-swap pass.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize all vertices as unlocked and set \(G_0=0\). At step \(t\), among unlocked \(a\in A\) and \(b\in B\), choose a pair maximizing the exact cut reduction \(g(a,b)\) produced by exchanging them; record the pair, lock both vertices, update the remaining gains, and set \(G_t=G_{t-1}+g(a,b)\). Continue until no unlocked cross-pair exists. Choose \(t^*\in\operatorname*{arg\,max}_t G_t\). If \(G_{t^*}>0\), commit precisely the first \(t^*\) recorded swaps; otherwise restore the initial partition. Repeat passes until a pass has no positive-gain prefix, and output the resulting balanced bipartition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Kernighan-Lin greedily locks cross-block vertex pairs, then commits the prefix of swaps giving the largest positive cumulative cut reduction.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E,w)\) is a finite weighted undirected graph.
An exactly balanced bipartition \((A,B)\) is given.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A pass outputs the best positive-gain prefix of locked pair exchanges, or leaves the partition unchanged when no prefix has positive gain.

notation.meaning: Cut reduction obtained by swapping \(a\) and \(b\).
Cumulative gain after the first \(t\) swaps.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: The locked maximum-gain pair-swap pass is the classical Kernighan-Lin refinement rule.

children.title: Fiduccia–Mattheyses Refinement
children.top_down_role: Single-vertex move refinement regimes with gain management.

knowledge_statements.title: Fiduccia–Mattheyses Refinement
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Balance-constrained two-way single-vertex refinement; bucket implementation details are abstracted.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize every vertex as unlocked and place each movable vertex in a gain structure keyed by its current cut reduction \(g(v)\). Repeatedly select an unlocked vertex of maximum gain whose move keeps the block weights within the permitted balance interval, move and lock it, update the gains of affected unlocked neighbors, and record the cumulative gain \(G_t\). Stop when no feasible unlocked move remains. Choose a recorded prefix maximizing \(G_t\); commit that prefix if its gain is positive and undo its suffix, otherwise undo the entire pass. Repeat passes until no positive-gain prefix exists, and output the final feasible bipartition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fiduccia-Mattheyses uses a gain structure for locked single-vertex moves and retains only the best feasible positive-gain prefix of each pass.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E,w)\) is a finite weighted graph or hypergraph.
A feasible bipartition and a permitted balance interval are given.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A pass commits the feasible prefix of locked single-vertex moves with maximum positive cumulative gain, or makes no change if none exists.

notation.meaning: Immediate cut reduction from moving vertex \(v\).
Cumulative gain of the first \(t\) recorded moves.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Gain ordering, locking, and best-prefix rollback define the classical Fiduccia-Mattheyses pass.

children.title: Refinement-Regime Comparison
children.top_down_role: Structural settings favoring pair-exchange or single-vertex refinement.

knowledge_statements.title: Refinement-Regime Comparison
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Comparison by move neighborhood and balance regime, excluding implementation-specific running-time claims.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a partition \(P\), Kernighan–Lin searches sequences drawn from \(N_{\mathrm{KL}}(P)\), where each elementary move exchanges one vertex from each block and therefore preserves equal cardinality. Fiduccia–Mattheyses searches sequences drawn from \(N_{\mathrm{FM}}(P)\), where each elementary move transfers one vertex and is feasible only when the resulting block weights remain within the balance interval. Consequently, a partition can be locally optimal for one neighborhood but not the other. Pair swaps directly explore compensated exchanges under exact balance, whereas single moves directly exploit available balance slack; best-prefix rollback permits both methods to traverse individually nonimproving moves within a pass.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Kernighan-Lin explores balance-preserving pair swaps, while Fiduccia-Mattheyses explores feasible single moves; their local optima therefore need not coincide.
assumptions_latex: Both methods refine a finite weighted bipartition using exact cut gains.
Kernighan–Lin enforces exact balance by pair swaps, while Fiduccia–Mattheyses permits feasible single-vertex moves within a balance interval.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The methods optimize different move neighborhoods; exact-balance pair swaps and tolerance-based single moves yield distinct local-optimality regimes.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: The comparison follows from the algorithms' distinct feasible move neighborhoods.

knowledge_statements.title: Flow-Based Partition Refinement
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Localized two-way refinement reduced to an auxiliary minimum terminal cut.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Construct an auxiliary capacitated network \(H\) with terminals \(s,t\) and one node for every vertex in \(R\). For each original edge with both endpoints in \(R\), add the corresponding capacity between its endpoint nodes. For every edge from \(u\in R\) to a fixed vertex outside \(R\), add its weight to the terminal capacity that charges assigning \(u\) to the opposite block. Compute a maximum \(s\)-\(t\) flow and an associated minimum \(s\)-\(t\) cut, and assign each vertex in \(R\) according to its terminal side. Accept the induced partition only if it satisfies the prescribed balance constraint and decreases cut weight; otherwise retain the input partition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Encode a local two-way reassignment as a terminal network, solve a minimum cut, and accept the induced partition only when balanced and improving.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E,w)\) is a finite undirected graph with nonnegative capacities.
A bipartition \((A,B)\) and a refinement region \(R\subseteq V\) are fixed.
Vertices in \(V\setminus R\) retain their current blocks.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A minimum terminal cut gives the least-capacity reassignment represented by the auxiliary network, and accepting only feasible improving candidates preserves refinement validity.

notation.meaning: Source and sink terminals representing the two fixed sides.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A proper \(k\)-coloring of \(G\) is a map \(c:V\to\{1,\ldots,k\}\) satisfying \(c(u)\ne c(v)\) for every \(uv\in E\). Chromatic optimization asks for a proper coloring using the minimum number of colors; its optimum is \[\chi(G)=\min\bigl\{k\in\mathbb Z_{\ge 0}:\exists c:V\to\{1,\ldots,k\},\ c(u)\ne c(v)\ \forall uv\in E\bigr\}.\] For \(V=\varnothing\), the convention is \(\chi(G)=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Chromatic optimization finds a proper vertex coloring using as few colors as possible; the optimum is the graph's chromatic number.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Weighted chromatic number
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition for an arbitrary graph with integral vertex weights, including the vertex-clique blow-up representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $G=(V,E)$ and $w:V\to\mathbb{Z}_{+}$. The weighted chromatic number $\chi(G,w)$ is the minimum $k$ such that stable sets $S_1,\ldots,S_k$ exist and each $i\in V$ belongs to $w_i$ of them. For $w\equiv1$, $\chi(G,w)=\chi(G)$. Equivalently, $\chi(G,w)$ is the chromatic number of the graph obtained by replacing each vertex $i$ by a clique of $w_i$ vertices.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The weighted chromatic number is the minimum number of stable sets in which each vertex appears according to its integer weight. Unit weights recover ordinary coloring, and the definition is equivalent to coloring the corresponding vertex-clique blow-up graph.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \chi(G,w)=\min\{k:\exists S_1,\ldots,S_k\text{ stable with }|\{j:i\in S_j\}|=w_i\ \forall i\in V\}.

children.title: Complexity-Separation Regimes
children.top_down_role: Graph classes where the two constraint models differ in complexity.

assumptions_latex: Inputs are finite simple graphs represented by adjacency lists.
The palette or lists are part of the explicit input.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Ordinary \(2\)-colorability and list coloring with lists of size at most \(2\) are polynomial-time decidable, whereas unrestricted list coloring is NP-complete.

notation.meaning: permitted color list at vertex v

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical decision-complexity boundary for explicit finite color domains.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Ordinary \(2\)-colorability is decidable in \(O(n+m)\) time by testing bipartiteness. If \(|L(v)|\le2\) for every \(v\), list-coloring feasibility reduces in polynomial time to \(2\)-SAT by introducing Boolean choices for two-element lists and clauses forbidding equal colors across edges. In contrast, unrestricted list-coloring feasibility belongs to \(\mathrm{NP}\) and is \(\mathrm{NP}\)-complete. Thus vertex-specific domains can change the complexity even though the local edge relation remains inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two-colorability is linear-time and list coloring with lists of size at most two reduces to 2-SAT, while unrestricted list coloring is NP-complete.
knowledge_statements.title: Complexity-Separation Regimes

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a proper coloring \(c:V\to\{1,\ldots,k\}\), let \(V_i=\{v\in V:c(v)=i\}\). The coloring is equitable when \(\bigl||V_i|-|V_j|\bigr|\le1\) for all \(i,j\). Equivalently, every color class has size in \(\{\lfloor n/k\rfloor,\lceil n/k\rceil\}\). Empty classes are permitted; consequently, when \(k>n\), equitability requires every nonempty class to be a singleton.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Stars exhibit an unbounded gap between ordinary and equitable chromatic numbers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the star \(S_n=K_{1,n}\), ordinary coloring gives \(\chi(S_n)=2\). In any proper coloring, the center's color class is a singleton and every other class contains only leaves. Equitability therefore forces each leaf-only class to contain at most two vertices. Hence at least \(\lceil n/2\rceil\) leaf colors and one center color are necessary, and partitioning the leaves into pairs and at most one singleton attains this bound. Consequently, \[\chi_{=}(S_n)=\left\lceil\frac n2\right\rceil+1,\] so \(\chi_{=}(S_n)-\chi(S_n)\) is unbounded.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Stars are 2-colorable, but equitable coloring of a star with n leaves needs one center color and at least ceiling(n/2) leaf colors.

knowledge_statements.title: List Edge Coloring
knowledge_statements.scope_note: List coloring applied to the edges of a finite simple graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite simple graph, and assign each edge \(e\in E\) a finite list \(L(e)\) of available colors. The list chromatic index \(\chi'_\ell(G)\) is the least integer \(k\) such that an \(L\)-edge-coloring exists for every list assignment satisfying \(|L(e)|\ge k\) for all \(e\in E\).

assumptions_latex: Each \(L(e)\) is a finite set of colors.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\chi'_\ell(G)=\min\{k: |L(e)|\ge k\ \forall e\in E\Rightarrow G\text{ has an }L\text{-edge-coloring}\}.\)

knowledge_statements.title: Total Coloring

The total chromatic number \(\chi''(G)\) is the minimum cardinality of a color set admitting such a coloring.

knowledge_statements.title: Circular Coloring
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Circular colorings represented as homomorphisms to circular clique graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let integers \(p,q\) satisfy \(p\ge 2q>0\). The circular clique \(K_{p/q}\) has vertex set \(\mathbb Z_p\), with \(ij\) an edge exactly when \(q\le |i-j|_p\le p-q\), where \(|i-j|_p=\min\{|i-j|,p-|i-j|\}\). A \((p,q)\)-coloring of a finite graph \(G\) is precisely a homomorphism \(G\to K_{p/q}\). Its circular chromatic number is \(\chi_c(G)=\inf\{p/q:G\to K_{p/q}\}\).

knowledge_statements.title: Greedy Ordering Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ordering-sensitive upper bound produced by sequential greedy vertex coloring.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(v_1,\ldots,v_n\) be an ordering of the vertices of a finite simple graph \(G\). Color the vertices sequentially, assigning to \(v_i\) the least positive color not already used on its earlier neighbors. If \(b_i=|N(v_i)\cap\{v_1,\ldots,v_{i-1}\}|\), then the resulting coloring is proper and uses at most \(1+\max_i b_i\) colors. Consequently, every ordering certifies \(\chi(G)\le 1+\max_i b_i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Greedy coloring along an ordering uses at most one more color than the largest number of earlier neighbors of any vertex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\chi(G)\le 1+\max_{1\le i\le n}|N(v_i)\cap\{v_1,\ldots,v_{i-1}\}|.\)

notation.meaning: number of neighbors of v_i preceding it

knowledge_statements.title: Degeneracy Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Chromatic bound obtained from a degeneracy ordering.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a nonempty finite simple graph \(G\), define its degeneracy by \(d(G)=\max_{\varnothing\ne H\subseteq G}\delta(H)\), where \(H\) ranges over subgraphs. Repeatedly deleting a vertex of current degree at most \(d(G)\) and reversing the deletion order gives an ordering in which every vertex has at most \(d(G)\) earlier neighbors. Greedy coloring in this order therefore yields \(\chi(G)\le d(G)+1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every d-degenerate graph has a deletion ordering that greedy coloring uses to produce at most d+1 colors.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is a nonempty finite simple graph.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\chi(G)\le d(G)+1\), where \(d(G)=\max_{\varnothing\ne H\subseteq G}\delta(H)\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The degeneracy definition, deletion ordering, and chromatic bound are mutually consistent, and theorem is the correct role for the leaf. The record lacks a supporting source and specific locator.

knowledge_statements.title: Bound-Tightness Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard graph families attaining the degeneracy coloring bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The degeneracy bound \(\chi(G)\le d(G)+1\) is sharp. For every integer \(d\ge 0\), the complete graph \(K_{d+1}\) satisfies \(d(K_{d+1})=d\) and \(\chi(K_{d+1})=d+1\). Further equality regimes include every forest containing an edge, for which \(d(G)=1\) and \(\chi(G)=2\), and every odd cycle, for which \(d(G)=2\) and \(\chi(G)=3\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Complete graphs, nontrivial forests, and odd cycles show that the degeneracy upper bound can be attained exactly.
assumptions_latex: All graphs considered are finite and simple.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\chi(K_{d+1})=d(K_{d+1})+1=d+1\) for every \(d\ge0\); equality also holds for nontrivial forests and odd cycles.

knowledge_statements.title: Critical-Graph Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural properties underlying vertex-critical coloring arguments.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A finite simple graph \(G\) is \(k\)-critical if \(\chi(G)=k\) and every proper subgraph is \((k-1)\)-colorable. Every \(k\)-critical graph is connected and has minimum degree at least \(k-1\). Indeed, for each vertex \(v\), every \((k-1)\)-coloring of \(G-v\) uses all \(k-1\) colors on \(N(v)\); otherwise that coloring extends to \(G\). For \(k\ge3\), a \(k\)-critical graph has no cut vertex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Minimal k-chromatic graphs are connected, have minimum degree at least k−1, and, for k≥3, have no cut vertex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G\text{ is connected}\), \(\delta(G)\ge k-1\), and \(k\ge3\Rightarrow G\text{ has no cut vertex}.\)

knowledge_statements.title: Clique Lower-Bound Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A directly verifiable lower-bound witness for vertex coloring.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite simple graph. A set \(Q\subseteq V\) is a clique certificate of value \(r\) when \(|Q|=r\) and every two distinct vertices in \(Q\) are adjacent. In every proper vertex coloring, vertices of \(Q\) receive pairwise distinct colors; hence the certificate establishes \(\chi(G)\ge r\). Given \(Q\), validity is checkable using at most \(\binom r2\) adjacency tests.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An r-vertex clique certifies that at least r colors are necessary, and the certificate is verified by checking all vertex pairs.
assumptions_latex: \(Q\subseteq V\), \(|Q|=r\), and \(uv\in E\) for all distinct \(u,v\in Q\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\chi(G)\ge r\), verifiable with at most \(\binom r2\) adjacency tests.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The clique witness directly certifies the chromatic lower bound, the adjacency-test count is correct, and certificate exactly fits the terminal container. The record nevertheless has no supporting source or inspectable locator.

knowledge_statements.title: Hadwiger Conjecture Family
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard minor-theoretic formulation; conjectural for general finite graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite simple graph \(G\), let \(h(G)\) be the largest integer \(t\) for which \(G\) contains the complete graph \(K_t\) as a minor. Hadwiger's conjecture asserts \(\chi(G)\le h(G)\). Equivalently, for every integer \(t\ge1\), every graph with \(\chi(G)\ge t\) is conjectured to contain a \(K_t\)-minor. This statement is not a theorem in general and must be treated as an open conjectural principle.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\chi(G)\le h(G)\), equivalently \(\chi(G)\ge t\Rightarrow K_t\preccurlyeq G\), is conjectured.

knowledge_statements.title: Planar Coloring Theorem Family
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Four-color bound and the triangle-free planar strengthening.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\) be a finite simple planar graph. The Four Color Theorem states that \(G\) has a proper vertex coloring with at most four colors, so \(\chi(G)\le4\). Under the additional hypothesis that \(G\) contains no triangle, Grötzsch's theorem strengthens the bound to \(\chi(G)\le3\). Both bounds are sharp: \(K_4\) is planar and requires four colors, while odd cycles are triangle-free planar graphs requiring three colors.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every planar graph is 4-colorable, and every triangle-free planar graph is 3-colorable; complete graphs and odd cycles show sharpness.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is a finite simple planar graph.
For the strengthened conclusion, \(G\) is triangle-free.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\chi(G)\le4\), and if \(G\) is triangle-free then \(\chi(G)\le3\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Four Color Theorem, the triangle-free planar strengthening, and the stated sharpness examples are mathematically consistent, while theorem fits the theorem-family container. The combined record requires target-specific citations and precise locators supporting both named theorems.

knowledge_statements.title: Kőnig Line-Coloring Family
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite bipartite multigraph form of Kőnig's line-coloring theorem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every finite bipartite multigraph without loops \(G=(U\cup W,E)\), the edge set admits a partition \(E=M_1\mathbin{\dot\cup}\cdots\mathbin{\dot\cup}M_{\Delta(G)}\) into matchings. Equivalently, there exists a map \(c:E\to\{1,\ldots,\Delta(G)\}\) such that \(c(e)\ne c(f)\) whenever distinct edges \(e\) and \(f\) share an endpoint. In particular, \(\chi'(G)=\Delta(G)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every finite bipartite multigraph without loops can be edge-colored with exactly its maximum degree many colors.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(U\cup W,E)\) is a finite bipartite multigraph without loops.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\chi'(G)=\Delta(G)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A finite simple graph \(G\) is called class two when no proper edge-coloring with \(\Delta(G)\) colors exists. knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every finite simple graph \(G\), define its chromatic index excess by \(s(G)=\chi'(G)-\Delta(G)\). Vizing's theorem gives \(s(G)\in\{0,1\}\). knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If a feasible coloring uses labels \(1,
\ldots,q\), every permutation in \(\mathfrak S_q\) produces an equivalent coloring. In an assignment model, constraints \(y_j\ge y_{j+1}\) for \(1\le j<q\), together with a first-occurrence precedence rule, select a canonical labeling without changing the optimum. knowledge_statements.scope_note: Regular-simplex Gram-matrix relaxation of finite graph \(k\)-colorability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider the semidefinite feasibility system \[X\succeq0,
\qquad X_{vv}=1\quad(v\in V),
\qquad X_{uv}=-\frac{1}{k-1}\quad(uv\in E).\] A proper \(k\)-coloring makes this system feasible by assigning to each color one vertex of a regular simplex in \(\mathbb R^{k-1}\) and taking \(X\) as the resulting Gram matrix. Therefore feasibility is necessary for \(k\)-colorability, and infeasibility is a certificate that \(\chi(G)>k\). Allowing the edge conditions as inequalities gives the corresponding vector-coloring relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proper k-coloring produces a positive-semidefinite Gram matrix from regular-simplex color vectors; infeasibility therefore rules out k-colorability.

knowledge_statements.title: Greedy Ordering Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential first-fit coloring under a prescribed vertex ordering.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite simple graph and let \((v_1,\ldots,v_n)\) order \(V\). For \(i=1,\ldots,n\), assign \(v_i\) the least positive integer not assigned to any earlier neighbor: \[c(v_i)=\min\bigl(\mathbb N_{>0}\setminus\{c(v_j):j<i,\ v_jv_i\in E\}\bigr).\] The output \(c\) is a proper coloring. If \(d_i^-\) is the number of neighbors of \(v_i\) preceding it, then the algorithm uses at most \(1+\max_i d_i^-\) colors.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Process vertices in order, giving each the smallest color absent from its earlier neighbors; the result is proper and uses at most one plus the maximum earlier-neighbor count.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(c\) is proper and \(|c(V)|\le 1+\max_i d_i^-\).

notation.meaning: number of neighbors of v_i occurring earlier in the ordering

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard first-fit coloring definition and ordering bound

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm content kind and local container fit, and the first-fit rule and ordering bound are standard. However, no citation or inspectable locator is supplied. Also, the expression \(\max_i d_i^-\) is undefined when \(V=\varnothing\); a source-backed version should either assume \(V\ne\varnothing\) or handle the empty graph separately.

children.title: Smallest-Last Methods
children.top_down_role: Degeneracy-oriented vertex orderings used for constructive coloring.

knowledge_statements.title: Smallest-Last Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Degeneracy ordering followed by reverse-order greedy coloring.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite simple graph. Repeatedly choose a minimum-degree vertex in the current induced graph, delete it, and record the deletion sequence \((w_1,\ldots,w_n)\). Then greedily color vertices in the reverse order \((w_n,\ldots,w_1)\). If \(d=\max_i\deg_{G[\{w_i,\ldots,w_n\}]}(w_i)\), the resulting coloring is proper and uses at most \(d+1\) colors; this \(d\) equals the degeneracy of \(G\). Ties may be resolved arbitrarily.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Delete a current minimum-degree vertex repeatedly, then greedily color in reverse deletion order. The method uses at most degeneracy plus one colors.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The reverse deletion ordering yields a proper coloring with at most \(d+1\) colors.

notation.meaning: degeneracy attained along the deletion sequence

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm content kind matches Smallest-Last Methods, and the stated deletion-order degeneracy guarantee is standard for a nonempty finite graph. No supporting citation or locator is provided, and the displayed maximum defining \(d\) needs an explicit nonempty-graph convention or hypothesis.

children.title: Recursive Largest-First Methods
children.top_down_role: Color-class construction based on recursive largest-first selection.

knowledge_statements.title: Recursive Largest-First Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: RLF constructs one independent color class at a time.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be finite and simple. While uncolored vertices remain, initialize a color class \(S\) with an uncolored vertex of maximum uncolored degree. Let \(A\) be uncolored vertices nonadjacent to every vertex of \(S\). While \(A\ne\varnothing\), add to \(S\) a vertex maximizing its number of uncolored neighbors outside \(A\), breaking ties by minimum degree in \(G[A]\), and recompute \(A\). Assign one new color to all vertices of \(S\), remove them, and repeat. Each produced \(S\) is independent, so the output is a proper coloring.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: RLF repeatedly grows an independent color class, favoring eligible vertices that exclude many remaining candidates, and removes each completed class before constructing the next.
assumptions_latex: All stated selection ties are resolved arbitrarily.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The generated color classes partition \(V\) into independent sets and therefore define a proper coloring.

notation.meaning: eligible uncolored vertices nonadjacent to S

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Algorithm is the correct knowledge kind for this leaf, but the exact RLF selection and tie-breaking variant lacks a source. The phrase "uncolored neighbors outside \(A\)" is state-dependent and does not explicitly distinguish vertices excluded by adjacency to \(S\) from vertices already placed in \(S\); an authoritative algorithm statement is needed to fix the intended candidate sets.

children.title: Constructive Ordering Regimes
children.top_down_role: Graph structures and performance patterns distinguishing the two ordering families.

knowledge_statements.title: Constructive Ordering Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ordering quality controls the color guarantee of sequential coloring.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite simple graph \(G=(V,E)\) and an ordering \(\pi=(v_1,\ldots,v_n)\), define its backward width by \[b(\pi)=\max_i|N(v_i)\cap\{v_1,\ldots,v_{i-1}\}|.\] Greedy coloring along \(\pi\) uses at most \(b(\pi)+1\) colors. Consequently, any constructive regime producing an ordering with \(b(\pi)\le k\) supplies a polynomially checkable certificate that its greedy coloring uses at most \(k+1\) colors. A reverse smallest-last ordering has backward width equal to at most the degeneracy of \(G\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Any constructed ordering with at most k earlier neighbors per vertex makes greedy coloring use at most k+1 colors; reverse smallest-last ordering realizes the degeneracy guarantee.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(|c_\pi(V)|\le b(\pi)+1\), and reverse smallest-last order has \(b(\pi)\le\operatorname{degen}(G)\).

notation.meaning: maximum number of earlier neighbors in ordering π

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: elementary greedy-ordering and degeneracy bounds

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Property is a reasonable primary kind for the ordering-width relation in this container, although the record also characterizes the ordering as a certificate. The greedy bound and reverse smallest-last claim are mathematically standard, but neither has a cited source or inspectable locator.

knowledge_statements.title: DSATUR Coloring
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential coloring ordered dynamically by saturation degree.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite simple graph. Initially all vertices are uncolored. At each iteration choose an uncolored vertex \(v\) maximizing the saturation degree \(\sigma(v)=|\{c(u):u\in N(v),\ u\text{ colored}\}|\); break ties by maximum degree in the uncolored subgraph, then arbitrarily. Assign \(v\) the least positive color absent from its colored neighborhood. Stop when every vertex is colored. The resulting map \(c:V\to\mathbb N_{>0}\) is a proper coloring.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeatedly color the vertex seeing the most distinct neighbor colors, using residual degree for ties and the smallest available color. The completed coloring is proper.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The procedure terminates after \(|V|\) assignments and returns a proper coloring \(c\).

notation.meaning: number of distinct colors present in the colored neighborhood of v
partial and ultimately complete vertex coloring

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits DSATUR Coloring and the construction yields a proper coloring. The residual-degree tie break is one DSATUR variant rather than a universally fixed definition, so the exact rule requires a specific source and locator.

children.title: Coloring Search-Tree Branching
children.top_down_role: Branching designs for exact coloring search trees.

knowledge_statements.title: Coloring Search-Tree Branching
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Complete branching scheme for exact fixed-\(k\) coloring feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a finite simple graph \(G=(V,E)\), an integer \(k\ge1\), and a proper partial coloring \(c:S\to\{1,\ldots,k\}\), choose an uncolored vertex \(v\in V\setminus S\). Its feasible colors are \[F(v)=\{1,\ldots,k\}\setminus\{c(u):u\in S\cap N(v)\}.\] Create one child for every \(a\in F(v)\), extending the assignment by \(c(v)=a\). A node with \(F(v)=\varnothing\) is infeasible; a node with \(S=V\) certifies feasibility. Exhausting all children without a complete assignment certifies that the parent has no \(k\)-coloring extension.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose an uncolored vertex and branch over every color not used by a colored neighbor. Empty domains fail; complete assignments certify k-colorability.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The children partition all proper \(k\)-coloring extensions of the current partial assignment.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits the branching leaf, and the children exhaust the extensions of the stated proper partial \(k\)-coloring. The record has no citation or inspectable locator supporting this exact search-tree formulation.

children.title: Coloring Bounds for Pruning
children.top_down_role: Upper and lower bounding mechanisms used to restrict exact search.

knowledge_statements.title: Coloring Bounds for Pruning
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lower and upper bounds certify safe branch-and-bound pruning.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At a node of an exact chromatic-number search, let \(L\) be a valid lower bound on every completion reachable from that node and let \(U\) be the number of colors in a known complete coloring of \(G\). Then \(L\le\chi(G)\le U\) at the root, and the node may be pruned whenever \(L\ge U\), since it cannot improve the incumbent. A clique \(Q\) compatible with the node gives the verifiable lower bound \(L\ge|Q|\); any explicit proper coloring gives the verifiable upper bound \(U=|c(V)|\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A compatible clique supplies a lower bound and a proper coloring an upper bound. A search node is safely discarded when its lower bound cannot beat the incumbent.
assumptions_latex: \(L\) bounds every completion at the node and \(U\) is an incumbent coloring value.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(L\ge U\), pruning the node preserves the optimal chromatic number.

notation.meaning: node lower bound on the attainable color count
clique used as a lower-bound certificate

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: branch-and-bound dominance and clique/coloring certificates

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Certificate is an appropriate kind for clique and incumbent bounds used in pruning. No supporting source is supplied. The sentence \(L\ge |Q|\) should also be sourced or restated as an update such as \(L\leftarrow\max\{L,|Q|\}\), because an arbitrary valid lower bound \(L\) need not already dominate the clique bound.

children.title: Coloring Search Pruning Regimes
children.top_down_role: Dominance, infeasibility, and structural pruning opportunities.

knowledge_statements.title: Coloring Search Pruning Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sound pruning predicates for partial exact-coloring search.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a search node represented by a proper partial coloring with color domains \(D(v)\) on uncolored vertices, pruning is sound if at least one of the following holds: \(D(v)=\varnothing\) for some uncolored \(v\); propagation derives a violated edge or cardinality constraint; a valid node lower bound \(L\) satisfies \(L\ge U\), where \(U\) is the incumbent value; or the node is dominated by an already explored equivalent state whose admissible completions include its own. Each predicate excludes every completion that could improve \(U\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Prune on an empty color domain, propagated contradiction, lower bound no better than the incumbent, or certified dominance by an equivalent state.
assumptions_latex: All propagation, bounding, and dominance tests are valid for the represented subtree.
\(U\) is the value of a known feasible coloring.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every node satisfying a listed predicate may be removed without eliminating a coloring better than \(U\).

notation.meaning: current feasible color domain of uncolored vertex v
node lower bound and incumbent upper bound

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard constraint and branch-and-bound pruning predicates

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Condition is the correct role for a list of pruning predicates. Empty domains, contradictions, and bound pruning are standard, but the dominance predicate does not state what information from the explored state certifies disposal of the dominated subtree. A specific source is required for that regime and none is cited for the other predicates.

children.title: Restricted Master Coloring Models
children.top_down_role: Restricted column formulations used during exact coloring search.

knowledge_statements.title: Restricted Master Coloring Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Set-covering restricted master problem for column-generation coloring.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be finite and simple, and let \(\mathcal S'\) be a finite collection of stable sets. The restricted master relaxation is \[\min\ \sum_{S\in\mathcal S'}x_S\quad\text{subject to}\quad \sum_{S\in\mathcal S':v\in S}x_S\ge1\ \ (v\in V),\qquad x_S\ge0\ \ (S\in\mathcal S').\] Requiring \(x_S\in\{0,1\}\) gives the restricted integer master. If \(\mathcal S'\) contains all stable sets, the integer optimum equals \(\chi(G)\); with fewer columns it is an upper restriction and may be infeasible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cover every vertex by selected stable-set columns while minimizing their number. With all stable sets and binary variables, the optimum is the chromatic number.
assumptions_latex: Every member of \(\mathcal S'\) is a stable set of \(G\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For the complete stable-set family \(\mathcal S\), the binary master optimum is \(\chi(G)\).

notation.meaning: current restricted family of stable-set columns
selection variable for stable-set column S

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard set-covering formulation of graph coloring

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Representation is the correct kind for this restricted-master formulation. The set-covering model and complete-family chromatic-number equivalence are standard and internally consistent, but no source or specific locator supports them.

children.title: Stable-Set Pricing Problems
children.top_down_role: Pricing subproblems that generate color-class columns.

knowledge_statements.title: Stable-Set Pricing Problems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pricing oracle for the set-covering coloring master relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the restricted master relaxation with dual multipliers \(\pi_v\ge0\) on the vertex-covering constraints, the reduced cost of a stable-set column \(S\) is \[\bar c_S=1-\sum_{v\in S}\pi_v.\] Hence pricing is the maximum-weight stable-set problem \[z(\pi)=\max\left\{\sum_{v\in S}\pi_v:S\subseteq V\text{ is stable}\right\}.\] A negative-reduced-cost column exists exactly when \(z(\pi)>1\). If \(z(\pi)\le1\), the current restricted-master solution is optimal for the full linear relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Using vertex dual prices as weights, solve a maximum-weight stable-set problem. A column improves the master exactly when its weight exceeds one.
assumptions_latex: The restricted master relaxation is feasible and solved to LP optimality.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(z(\pi)>1\) yields an improving column, while \(z(\pi)\le1\) certifies full-master LP optimality.

notation.meaning: dual multiplier for covering vertex v
reduced cost of stable-set column S
maximum dual weight of a stable set

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: LP duality for set-covering column generation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Duality is the correct kind for the pricing relation, and the reduced-cost sign and threshold are consistent with the stated minimization covering master. The exact full-master optimality claim has no cited source or inspectable locator.

children.title: Pricing-Compatible Branching
children.top_down_role: Branching structures that preserve tractable or reusable pricing subproblems.

knowledge_statements.title: Pricing-Compatible Branching
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ryan–Foster-style branching that preserves stable-set pricing structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At a fractional coloring master solution, choose distinct nonadjacent vertices \(u,v\) for which \(\sum_{S\ni u,v}x_S\) is fractional. Create two exhaustive branches. In the together branch, retain only columns \(S\) satisfying \(u\in S\iff v\in S\). In the separate branch, retain only columns satisfying \(|S\cap\{u,v\}|\le1\). Apply the same restrictions when generating new stable-set columns. Every integral coloring satisfies exactly one branch, and pricing remains a maximum-weight stable-set problem with the corresponding together-or-separate restriction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Branch on whether two nonadjacent vertices share a color. Restrict both existing and generated stable-set columns accordingly, preserving exhaustive search and structured pricing.
assumptions_latex: The master columns represent stable color classes.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The two branches cover all integral colorings and preserve constrained stable-set pricing.

notation.meaning: master variable for stable-set column S

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Ryan–Foster-style branching for set-partitioning or covering columns

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Algorithm is appropriate for the pricing-compatible branching leaf. The together/separate restrictions are plausible Ryan-Foster-style rules, but their use with the stated set-covering coloring master, the fractional branching quantity, and preservation of the pricing problem require a coloring-specific source and locator.

children.title: Integer Programming Encodings
children.top_down_role: Integer optimization encodings for exact graph coloring.

knowledge_statements.title: Integer Programming Encodings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Binary assignment formulation of the chromatic-number problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be finite and simple and set \(K=|V|\). For \(v\in V\) and \(c\in\{1,\ldots,K\}\), let \(x_{vc}\) indicate assignment of color \(c\), and let \(y_c\) indicate its use. Then \[\min\sum_{c=1}^K y_c\] subject to \[\sum_{c=1}^Kx_{vc}=1,\quad x_{vc}\le y_c,\quad x_{uc}+x_{vc}\le1\ \ (uv\in E),\quad x_{vc},y_c\in\{0,1\}\] encodes proper colorings. Its optimum equals \(\chi(G)\). The optional inequalities \(y_c\ge y_{c+1}\) remove color-label symmetry without changing the optimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Binary variables assign one color to each vertex, forbid equal colors across edges, and activate used colors. Minimizing activations yields the chromatic number.
assumptions_latex: The available color index set has size \(K=|V|\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The integer-program optimum is \(\chi(G)\).

notation.meaning: binary assignment of color c to vertex v
binary indicator that color c is used

source_refs.locator: Chapter 5. Integer Programming p. 103

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 5. Integer Programming p. 103

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Representation is the correct kind, and the binary formulation is mathematically standard. The cited locator identifies only a general integer-programming chapter and does not specifically support the graph-coloring formulation or symmetry inequalities. Full-text support is pending. In addition, the constraint display should explicitly quantify \(v\in V\), \(c\in\{1,\ldots,K\}\), and \(uv\in E\) for the respective constraint families.

children.title: SAT Encodings
children.top_down_role: Boolean satisfiability encodings for coloring feasibility and optimization.

knowledge_statements.title: SAT Encodings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Direct CNF encoding of fixed-k-colorability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite simple graph and let \(k\ge 1\). Introduce a Boolean variable \(x_{v,c}\) for every \(v\in V\) and \(c\in\{1,\ldots,k\}\). Form the CNF formula \(F_k(G)\) containing
\[
\bigvee_{c=1}^{k}x_{v,c}\quad(v\in V),
\]
\[
\neg x_{v,c}\vee\neg x_{v,d}\quad(v\in V,\ c<d),
\]
and
\[
\neg x_{u,c}\vee\neg x_{v,c}\quad(uv\in E,\ 1\le c\le k).
\]
Then \(F_k(G)\) is satisfiable if and only if \(G\) has a proper coloring using at most \(k\) colors; satisfying assignments and such colorings translate directly in polynomial time.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Vertex-color variables, exactly-one color clauses, and edge-conflict clauses form a satisfiable CNF exactly when the graph is k-colorable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F_k(G)\text{ is satisfiable}\iff \chi(G)\le k.\)

notation.meaning: Boolean variable asserting that vertex v receives color c.

children.title: Constraint-Programming Encodings
children.top_down_role: Constraint-programming representations for exact coloring.

knowledge_statements.title: Constraint-Programming Encodings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-domain constraint model for fixed-k-colorability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a finite simple graph \(G=(V,E)\) and \(k\ge1\), introduce one finite-domain variable \(C_v\) for each \(v\in V\), with domain \(\{1,\ldots,k\}\). Post the binary disequality constraint
\[
C_u\ne C_v
\]
for every edge \(uv\in E\). Equivalently, these constraints may be grouped as an all-different constraint on each clique, provided every edge constraint is represented. The constraint network has a feasible assignment if and only if \(G\) admits a proper coloring with at most \(k\) colors, and every feasible assignment specifies such a coloring.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Assign each vertex a finite-domain color variable and impose disequality across every edge; feasible assignments are precisely proper k-colorings.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists(C_v)_{v\in V}\text{ satisfying all constraints}\iff\chi(G)\le k.\)

notation.meaning: Finite-domain color variable for vertex v.

knowledge_statements.title: Decomposition-Based Dynamic Programming
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact fixed-k coloring over a supplied tree decomposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a finite graph \(G\), an integer \(k\ge1\), and a rooted nice tree decomposition \((T,\{B_t\})\) of width \(w\). For each node \(t\), store all proper maps \(\varphi:B_t\to\{1,\ldots,k\}\) extendible to the vertices introduced in the subtree of \(t\). At introduce nodes, retain maps respecting newly exposed edges; at forget nodes, project over the forgotten vertex; at join nodes, intersect the two child tables on their common bag. Accept exactly when the root table is nonempty. Back-pointers recover a coloring. The running time is \(O(|V(T)|k^{w+1}\operatorname{poly}(w))\), with \(O(k^{w+1})\) table space per processed node.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dynamic programming stores extendible bag colorings, combines them along a nice tree decomposition, and decides k-colorability in time exponential only in the width.
assumptions_latex: \((T,\{B_t\})\) is a supplied nice tree decomposition of \(G\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G\text{ is accepted}\iff\chi(G)\le k\), with time \(O(|V(T)|k^{w+1}\operatorname{poly}(w))\).

notation.meaning: Width of the supplied tree decomposition.
A proper coloring of a current bag.

knowledge_statements.title: Promised-Colorable Graph Approximation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Approximation guarantee under a promised chromatic-number upper bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Fix a promise parameter \(k\ge2\). A polynomial-time \(\rho\)-approximate coloring algorithm for promised \(k\)-colorable graphs is an algorithm that, on every finite \(n\)-vertex graph \(G\) satisfying \(\chi(G)\le k\), outputs a proper coloring of \(G\) using at most
\[
\rho(n,k)\,\chi(G)
\]
colors. A commonly used weaker bicriteria guarantee requires only at most \(f(n,k)\) colors under the same promise. No output guarantee is imposed on graphs violating the promise, although the algorithm must still halt in polynomial time on every encoded input.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The input is promised k-colorable, and the algorithm must efficiently return a proper coloring with a stated multiplicative or bicriteria color bound.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is a finite graph on \(n\) vertices.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\text{number of output colors}\le\rho(n,k)\chi(G)\), or \(\le f(n,k)\) for a bicriteria guarantee.

notation.meaning: Multiplicative approximation factor under the promise.
Bicriteria upper bound on output colors.

knowledge_statements.title: Semidefinite Coloring Rounding
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Randomized rounding of a feasible vector-coloring solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Input unit vectors \((u_v)_{v\in V}\) satisfying \(\langle u_v,u_w\rangle\le-1/(k-1)\) for every edge \(vw\in E\), together with an integer \(r\ge1\). Sample independent standard Gaussian vectors \(g_1,\ldots,g_r\) and assign
\[
c(v)=\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{1\le i\le r}\langle g_i,u_v\rangle,
\]
breaking ties deterministically. Mark every vertex incident to a monochromatic edge, retain the induced proper coloring on the unmarked vertices, and pass the marked induced subgraph to a specified repair or recursive coloring procedure. The output is proper when the repair uses colors disjoint from \(\{1,\ldots,r\}\); approximation bounds require a separate estimate on the marked set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Random Gaussian directions round vector colors; conflicting vertices are removed and repaired separately, producing a proper coloring when fresh repair colors are used.
assumptions_latex: The displayed vector-coloring constraints are feasible.
The repair procedure returns a proper coloring of the marked subgraph.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(c\) is proper on unmarked vertices, and combining it with disjoint repair colors gives a proper coloring of \(G\).

notation.meaning: Unit vector assigned to vertex v by the semidefinite relaxation.
Rounded preliminary color of vertex v.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Polynomial-time coloring of 3-colorable graphs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Semidefinite coloring-rounding guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every 3-colorable graph \(G\) on \(n\) vertices, a proper coloring of \(G\) using \(O(\sqrt n)\) colors can be found in polynomial time.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every 3-colorable n-vertex graph can be properly colored with O(sqrt(n)) colors in polynomial time.
assumptions_latex: G\text{ is a 3-colorable graph on }n\text{ vertices}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{A proper }O(\sqrt n)\text{-coloring of }G\text{ is computable in polynomial time}
