knowledge_statements.title: Local-Lemma Coloring Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Symmetric Lovász-local-lemma criterion for random list coloring.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,E)\) have maximum degree \(\Delta\), and suppose every vertex \(v\) has a list \(L(v)\) of exactly \(q\) colors. Choose each vertex color independently and uniformly from its list. For each edge \(uv\), let \(A_{uv}\) be the event that the endpoints receive the same color. Then \(\Pr(A_{uv})\le1/q\), and each event depends on at most \(2\Delta-2\) other edge events. Consequently, if
\[
e(2\Delta-1)\le q,
\]
the symmetric Lovász local lemma implies positive probability that no bad event occurs; hence \(G\) has a proper coloring from the prescribed lists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Independent random list colors yield a proper coloring with positive probability when the symmetric local-lemma dependency criterion holds.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G\) admits a proper coloring \(c\) with \(c(v)\in L(v)\) for every \(v\).

notation.meaning: Allowed color list at vertex v.
Bad event that adjacent vertices u and v receive one common color.

knowledge_statements.title: Chromatic-Number Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical complexity boundary for unrestricted finite graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For each fixed integer \(k\ge3\), the decision problem
\[
\text{given }G,\text{ decide whether }\chi(G)\le k
\]
is NP-complete. Membership in NP follows because a vertex-to-color assignment is polynomially verifiable. NP-hardness for \(k=3\) is the classical graph 3-colorability result; for every fixed \(k>3\), adjoining a clique of size \(k-3\) adjacent to every original vertex transfers 3-colorability to \(k\)-colorability. Therefore computing the exact chromatic number of an unrestricted finite graph is NP-hard. In contrast, the cases \(k=1\) and \(k=2\) are decidable in polynomial time.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fixed k-colorability is NP-complete for every k at least three, while one- and two-colorability are polynomial-time decidable; exact chromatic number is NP-hard.
assumptions_latex: Graphs are finite, simple, and represented explicitly.
\(k\) is fixed rather than part of the input.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(k\text{-COLORABILITY is NP-complete for fixed }k\ge3\), and exact computation of \(\chi(G)\) is NP-hard.

knowledge_statements.title: Coloring Inapproximability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard near-polynomial inapproximability threshold for chromatic number.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every constant \(\varepsilon>0\), unless \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\), no polynomial-time algorithm can, on every finite \(n\)-vertex graph \(G\), output a proper coloring using at most
\[
n^{1-\varepsilon}\chi(G)
\]
colors. Equivalently, under the same assumption, the chromatic number cannot be approximated within a factor \(n^{1-\varepsilon}\) in polynomial time. The guarantee concerns worst-case unrestricted graphs and multiplicative approximation measured against the optimum chromatic number; it does not rule out stronger guarantees on promised or structurally restricted graph classes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Unless P equals NP, unrestricted chromatic number has no polynomial-time approximation within n raised to one minus any fixed positive constant.
assumptions_latex: The input is an unrestricted finite graph on \(n\) vertices.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: No polynomial-time \(n^{1-\varepsilon}\)-approximation for \(\chi(G)\) exists.

notation.meaning: Number of vertices in the input graph.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: R-CLIQUE Gap Implication for the Extension's Clique Cover Number
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A quantified reduction-gadget implication used in the coloring-inapproximability setting; R-CLIQUE and the extension retain their source-defined meanings.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $H$ be an $r\times k$ graph such that $\omega(\widetilde H)=\omega(H)$. Then, for every $\rho>1$,
\[
\operatorname{R\text{-}CLIQUE}(H)<\frac{1}{\rho}\;\Longrightarrow\;\bar\chi(\widetilde H)>k\rho.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If H is an r-by-k graph and H and its extension have the same clique number, then for every rho greater than one, an R-CLIQUE value below 1/rho implies that the extension's clique cover number is greater than k times rho.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{R\text{-}CLIQUE}(H)<\frac{1}{\rho}\Rightarrow\bar\chi(\widetilde H)>k\rho.

children.title: List-Coloring Complexity

knowledge_statements.title: List-Coloring Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: NP-completeness of fixed-size list coloring on unrestricted graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix an integer \(k\ge3\). The problem of deciding whether a finite graph \(G\), supplied with a list \(L(v)\) of exactly \(k\) permitted colors for each vertex \(v\), has a proper list coloring is NP-complete. It belongs to NP because a proposed coloring can be checked against all lists and edges in polynomial time. NP-hardness already holds for instances with the identical list \(L(v)=\{1,\ldots,k\}\) at every vertex, since those instances are exactly the ordinary fixed-\(k\) colorability problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For every fixed list size at least three, deciding list-colorability is NP-complete, even when every vertex receives the same list.
assumptions_latex: Every input list has exactly \(k\) colors.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Fixed-\(k\) LIST-COLORABILITY is NP-complete.

notation.meaning: Set of colors permitted at vertex v.

children.title: Edge-Coloring Complexity

knowledge_statements.title: Edge-Coloring Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp NP-completeness result for cubic graph edge coloring.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a finite simple cubic graph \(G\), deciding whether its edges admit a proper coloring with three colors is NP-complete. Because every cubic graph has maximum degree \(\Delta(G)=3\) and Vizing's theorem gives \(\chi'(G)\in\{3,4\}\), this is equivalently the problem of deciding whether \(G\) is Class 1 rather than Class 2. A proposed three-edge-coloring is verifiable in polynomial time by checking that every pair of incident edges receives distinct colors. Consequently, computing the edge-chromatic number remains NP-hard even on cubic simple graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Determining whether a cubic simple graph has edge-chromatic number three is NP-complete, so exact edge coloring is NP-hard on cubic graphs.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is a finite simple cubic graph.
Proper edge colorings assign distinct colors to incident edges.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Deciding whether \(\chi'(G)=3\) is NP-complete; computing \(\chi'(G)\) on cubic graphs is NP-hard.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: NP-completeness of 3-edge-colorability at maximum degree three

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For graphs with maximum degree exactly 3, deciding whether a 3-edge-coloring exists is NP-complete.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Deciding whether }G\text{ is }3\text{-edge-colorable is NP-complete.}

knowledge_statements.title: Cross-Variant Complexity Transfers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Line-graph transfer between edge-coloring and vertex-coloring variants.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a finite simple graph \(H\), let its line graph \(L(H)\) have one vertex for each edge of \(H\), with two vertices adjacent exactly when their corresponding edges share an endpoint. Then, for every \(k\ge1\),
\[
H\text{ has a proper }k\text{-edge-coloring}\iff L(H)\text{ has a proper }k\text{-vertex-coloring}.
\]
Moreover, assigning each edge \(e\) a color list \(S(e)\) yields the identical list-coloring instance on \(L(H)\). The construction is polynomial in the explicit graph size, so decision and optimization reductions transfer from edge-coloring or list-edge-coloring to vertex-coloring or list-coloring restricted to line graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The line graph turns edges into vertices and preserves ordinary and list coloring, giving polynomial-time transfers between edge and vertex variants.
assumptions_latex: The line graph is represented explicitly.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\chi'(H)=\chi(L(H))\), and list-edge-colorings of \(H\) equal list-colorings of \(L(H)\) under corresponding lists.

notation.meaning: Permitted color list for edge e.

children.title: Bipartite Graph Coloring
children.top_down_role: Coloring structure, recognition context, and tractable regimes for bipartite graphs.

knowledge_statements.title: Bipartite Graph Coloring
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear-time two-coloring and odd-cycle certification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a finite undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\). For every unvisited connected component, choose a root, assign it color \(0\), and perform breadth-first search. Whenever an edge \(uv\) reaches an uncolored vertex \(v\), set \(c(v)=1-c(u)\); if an edge has \(c(u)=c(v)\), use the two search-tree paths to their lowest common ancestor together with \(uv\) to output an odd cycle. If no conflict occurs, \(c\) is a proper two-coloring. Thus the algorithm certifies either bipartiteness or non-bipartiteness in time \(O(|V|+|E|)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Breadth-first search alternates two colors in each component and returns either a proper two-coloring or an odd cycle witnessing failure.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite undirected graph represented by adjacency lists.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The algorithm outputs either a proper two-coloring of \(G\) or an odd cycle, in \(O(|V|+|E|)\) time.

notation.meaning: Binary color assigned to vertex v.

knowledge_statements.title: Chordal Graph Coloring
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Optimal greedy coloring from a perfect elimination ordering of a finite chordal graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be chordal, and let \(v_1,\ldots,v_n\) be a perfect elimination ordering, so the later neighbors of each \(v_i\) form a clique. Process the vertices in the reverse order \(v_n,\ldots,v_1\), assigning each vertex the smallest positive color unused by its already colored neighbors. The resulting coloring is proper and uses exactly \(\omega(G)=\chi(G)\) colors. Given the ordering and adjacency lists, the coloring can be implemented in polynomial time; a perfect elimination ordering can also be recognized and constructed in linear time.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Reverse greedy coloring along a perfect elimination ordering colors every chordal graph optimally, using exactly its clique number of colors.

\(v_1,\ldots,v_n\) is a perfect elimination ordering of \(G\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\text{reverse-greedy}(G)=\chi(G)=\omega(G)\).

children.title: Structural Tractability Contrast

knowledge_statements.title: Structural Tractability Contrast
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Contrasts the structural certificates underlying polynomial coloring of bipartite and chordal graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite simple graph \(G\), bipartiteness supplies a partition \(V(G)=A\mathbin{\dot\cup}B\) into stable sets, yielding \(\chi(G)\leq 2\), with equality when \(E(G)\neq\varnothing\). Chordality instead supplies a perfect elimination ordering; reverse greedy coloring along that ordering yields \(\chi(G)=\omega(G)\). Thus both classes admit polynomial-time optimal coloring, but through different certificates: parity-compatible bipartition for bipartite graphs and clique-structured elimination for chordal graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Bipartite coloring is certified by a two-part partition, whereas chordal coloring is certified by a perfect elimination ordering and clique structure.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is a finite simple graph belonging to the stated graph class.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G\text{ bipartite}\Rightarrow\chi(G)\leq2\), while \(G\text{ chordal}\Rightarrow\chi(G)=\omega(G)\) via reverse greedy elimination.

knowledge_statements.title: Interval Graph Coloring
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Optimal coloring from an interval representation using the chordal elimination order.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\) be the intersection graph of closed intervals \(I_v=[\ell_v,r_v]\). Order the vertices by nondecreasing right endpoint, breaking ties arbitrarily; this is a perfect elimination ordering. Greedily color in the reverse of this order, always choosing the smallest color absent from already colored neighbors. The coloring is optimal and uses \(\chi(G)=\omega(G)\) colors, where \(\omega(G)=\max_{t\in\mathbb R}|\{v:t\in I_v\}|\). Sorting endpoints followed by greedy coloring gives a polynomial-time implementation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sorting intervals by right endpoint gives an elimination order whose reverse greedy coloring uses exactly the maximum overlap number.
assumptions_latex: \(\{I_v:v\in V(G)\}\) is an interval representation of \(G\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\chi(G)=\omega(G)=\max_{t\in\mathbb R}|\{v:t\in I_v\}|\).

knowledge_statements.title: Permutation Graph Coloring
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Optimal coloring through the inversion-poset representation of a permutation graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G_\pi\) have vertices \(1,\ldots,n\), with \(ij\in E(G_\pi)\) exactly when \(i<j\) and \(\pi(i)>\pi(j)\). A color class is precisely an increasing subsequence of \(\pi\). Therefore a proper coloring is a partition of \(\pi\) into increasing subsequences, and a minimum such partition can be constructed by a chain-partition algorithm for the associated order. Its number of colors equals the length of a longest decreasing subsequence, which is also \(\omega(G_\pi)\); hence \(\chi(G_\pi)=\omega(G_\pi)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Coloring a permutation graph is equivalent to partitioning its permutation into increasing subsequences; the optimum equals the longest decreasing subsequence length.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\chi(G_\pi)=\omega(G_\pi)=\operatorname{LDS}(\pi)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Comparability Graph Coloring
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Optimal coloring of a comparability graph using ranks in an inducing partial order.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P=(V,\prec)\) be a finite partially ordered set and let \(G(P)\) join two distinct elements exactly when they are comparable. Define \(r(v)\) as the maximum cardinality of a chain ending at \(v\), and color \(v\) by \(r(v)\). If \(u\prec v\), then \(r(u)<r(v)\), so this is a proper coloring. It uses \(h(P)\) colors, where \(h(P)\) is the maximum chain cardinality. Every maximum chain is a clique, hence \(\chi(G(P))=\omega(G(P))=h(P)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Rank each poset element by the longest chain ending there; these ranks optimally color its comparability graph.

\(G(P)\) is the comparability graph induced by \(P\).

knowledge_statements.title: Representation-Based Class Relations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Class inclusions and equivalences relevant to representation-based coloring algorithms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For finite simple graphs, every interval graph is chordal. A graph is a permutation graph exactly when both it and its complement are comparability graphs. Consequently interval graphs, permutation graphs, and comparability graphs are perfect, although their certificates differ: interval intersection models yield endpoint elimination, permutation diagrams yield simultaneous comparability orientations of the graph and complement, and posets yield transitive orientations. These representations support polynomial-time optimal coloring but do not make the three named classes identical.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Interval graphs are chordal; permutation graphs are exactly graphs whose graph and complement are comparability graphs, and all three classes are perfect.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G\text{ interval}\Rightarrow G\text{ chordal}\), and \(G\text{ permutation}\Longleftrightarrow G,\overline G\text{ comparability}\).

knowledge_statements.title: Bounded-Width Graphs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact coloring parameterized by the width of a supplied tree decomposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\) have \(n\) vertices and a supplied tree decomposition of width at most \(k\). For any integer \(q\geq1\), dynamic programming over a nice form of the decomposition stores the proper color assignments of each bag and decides \(q\)-colorability in time \(O(nq^{k+1}\operatorname{poly}(k))\) and space \(O(q^{k+1}\operatorname{poly}(k))\). Since every graph of treewidth at most \(k\) is \((k+1)\)-colorable, testing \(q=1,\ldots,k+1\) determines \(\chi(G)\); thus coloring is polynomial-time solvable for fixed \(k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A width-k tree decomposition supports exact coloring by bag dynamic programming, with exponential dependence confined to k.

A tree decomposition of \(G\) of width at most \(k\) is supplied.

knowledge_statements.title: Greedy Ordering Sensitivity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Crown graphs exhibit an unbounded gap between good and bad greedy vertex orders.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(n\geq2\), let \(G_n\) be the crown graph with bipartition \(\{a_1,\ldots,a_n\}\) and \(\{b_1,\ldots,b_n\}\), containing every cross-edge except \(a_ib_i\). Then \(\chi(G_n)=2\). Under the greedy order \(a_1,b_1,a_2,b_2,\ldots,a_n,b_n\), first-fit assigns both \(a_i\) and \(b_i\) color \(i\), and therefore uses \(n\) colors. Hence the number of colors produced by greedy coloring cannot be bounded as a function of \(\chi(G)\) independently of the vertex order.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bipartite crown graph needs two colors, yet a bad alternating vertex order makes first-fit greedy use arbitrarily many colors.
assumptions_latex: Greedy coloring uses the smallest available positive integer color.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\chi(G_n)=2\) but \(\operatorname{FirstFit}(G_n;a_1,b_1,\ldots,a_n,b_n)=n\).

knowledge_statements.title: Color Symmetry Pathologies
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Orbit multiplicity in labeled-color assignment formulations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In a labeled \(k\)-color assignment formulation with variables \(x_{vc}\), every permutation \(\sigma\in S_k\) maps a feasible assignment to another by \(x'_{v,c}=x_{v,\sigma^{-1}(c)}\), without changing feasibility or any color-symmetric objective. If a coloring uses exactly \(r\) nonempty color classes, then it has \(k!/(k-r)!\) distinct labeled encodings obtained by injectively assigning those classes to the \(k\) labels. Thus one combinatorial coloring may generate a large orbit of equivalent integer solutions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Permuting color labels creates many equivalent assignment solutions; an r-class coloring has k!/(k-r)! labeled encodings among k colors.
assumptions_latex: Constraints and objective are invariant under permutations of the \(k\) color labels.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(|\operatorname{Orb}(x)|=k!/(k-r)!\) for a coloring with \(r\) nonempty classes.

children.title: Coloring Relaxation Weakness
children.top_down_role: Sources and regimes of weak bounds in coloring relaxations.

knowledge_statements.title: Coloring Relaxation Weakness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unbounded integrality gap in a standard color-indexed linear relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider the formulation with \(x_{vc},y_c\in\{0,1\}\), objective \(\min\sum_{c=1}^k y_c\), constraints \(\sum_c x_{vc}=1\), and \(x_{uc}+x_{vc}\leq y_c\) for every edge \(uv\) and color \(c\). Relax the variables to \([0,1]\). For \(G=K_n\) and \(k=n\), the assignment \(x_{vc}=1/n\) and \(y_c=2/n\) is feasible and has value \(2\), whereas every integer solution has value \(n\). The relaxation therefore has integrality gap at least \(n/2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a complete graph, the standard color-indexed LP can have value two although the integer chromatic number is n.

knowledge_statements.title: Maximum Cardinality Clique
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unweighted maximum-clique optimization in a finite simple graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a finite simple graph \(G=(V,E)\), a set \(C\subseteq V\) is a clique when every two distinct vertices in \(C\) are adjacent. The maximum cardinality clique problem is
\[\text{maximize }|C|\quad\text{subject to }C\subseteq V\text{ and }\{u,v\}\in E\text{ for all distinct }u,v\in C.\]
Any feasible set attaining the optimum is a maximum clique, and the optimum value is the clique number \(\omega(G)\). Maximality under inclusion is not sufficient for maximum cardinality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A maximum cardinality clique is a largest vertex set whose distinct pairs are all adjacent; its size is the clique number.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\omega(G)=\max\{|C|:C\subseteq V,\ \{u,v\}\in E\text{ for all distinct }u,v\in C\}\).

knowledge_statements.title: Maximum-Weight Clique
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Optimization definition for a finite, vertex-weighted simple graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite simple graph and let \(w:V\to\mathbb{R}\). A clique is a set \(C\subseteq V\) such that \(uv\in E\) for every two distinct vertices \(u,v\in C\). Its weight is \(w(C)=\sum_{v\in C}w(v)\). The maximum-weight clique value and solution set are
\[\omega_w(G)=\max\{w(C):C\subseteq V,\ C\text{ is a clique}\},\qquad \operatorname{MWC}(G,w)=\operatorname*{argmax}_{C\text{ clique}}w(C).\]
The empty clique is permitted and has weight \(0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Find a clique whose total vertex weight is largest; the empty clique is allowed, so the optimum is nonnegative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\omega_w(G)=\max\{\sum_{v\in C}w(v):C\text{ is a clique of }G\}\).

notation.meaning: sum of the weights of vertices in C

knowledge_statements.title: Weighted Clique Regime Transfers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Integer-weight vertex replication reduces weighted clique to cardinality clique.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,E)\) and \(w:V\to\mathbb{Z}_{>0}\). Construct \(G^w\) by replacing each \(v\in V\) with a clique \(K_v\) of \(w(v)\) copies. For distinct \(u,v\), join every vertex of \(K_u\) to every vertex of \(K_v\) exactly when \(uv\in E\). Then
\[\omega(G^w)=\omega_w(G).\]
Moreover, a clique \(C\) of \(G\) lifts to \(\bigcup_{v\in C}K_v\), while every maximum clique of \(G^w\) projects to a clique of \(G\) having the same weight.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Positive integer vertex weights can be encoded by clique modules, preserving the optimum and permitting solution projection in both directions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\omega(G^w)=\omega_w(G)\), with weight-preserving lifting and projection of optimal cliques.

notation.meaning: the clique module replacing vertex v

knowledge_statements.title: Maximal-Clique Enumeration
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Output-sensitive enumeration task for inclusion-maximal cliques.

For a finite simple graph \(G=(V,E)\), define
\[\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{cl}}(G)=\{C\subseteq V:C\text{ is a clique and no }v\in V\setminus C\text{ makes }C\cup\{v\}\text{ a clique}\}.\]
Maximal-clique enumeration is the task of outputting every member of \(\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{cl}}(G)\) exactly once and no other set. Maximality is inclusion-wise and does not mean that \(|C|\) is maximum.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{cl}}(G)\) is precisely the required output family.

Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite simple graph. A stable set is a subset \(S\subseteq V\) satisfying \(uv\notin E\) for all distinct \(u,v\in S\). The stability number and family of maximum stable sets are
\[\alpha(G)=\max\{|S|:S\subseteq V,\ S\text{ is stable}\},\qquad \operatorname{MSS}(G)=\{S:S\text{ is stable and }|S|=\alpha(G)\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Find a largest vertex subset containing no adjacent pair; its cardinality is the graph's stability number.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\alpha(G)=\max\{|S|:S\subseteq V,\ S\text{ is stable}\}\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Maximum-cardinality independent-set formulation and weakness of its edge LP relaxation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The binary edge-inequality formulation for maximum-cardinality independent set and its complete-graph relaxation failure boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a finite undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\), a set \(I\subseteq V\) is independent (stable) if no edge has both endpoints in \(I\). Maximum independent set is represented by
\[
\max \sum_{v\in V}x_v\quad\text{s.t.}\quad x_u+x_v\le 1\quad(\{u,v\}\in E),\qquad x_v\in\{0,1\}\quad(v\in V),
\]
with \(I^*=\{v\in V:x_v^*=1\}\) for an optimal solution \(x^*\). After replacing integrality by \(0\le x_v\le1\), the assignment \(x_v=\tfrac12\) is feasible, so \(z_{LP}(G)\ge |V|/2\). For \(G=K_n\) with \(n\ge2\), \(\alpha(K_n)=1\) while \(z_{LP}(K_n)\ge n/2\); hence this relaxation has an unbounded multiplicative gap on complete graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An independent or stable set contains no adjacent pair of vertices. Its maximum cardinality is modeled with one binary variable per vertex and an inequality allowing at most one endpoint of every edge to be selected. The unit-interval relaxation always admits the all-one-half solution. On complete graphs, the integer optimum is one while the relaxation value is at least half the number of vertices, so the relaxation gap grows without bound.
assumptions_latex: G=(V,E)\text{ is a finite undirected graph.}
x_v\in\{0,1\}\text{ in the integer formulation; }0\le x_v\le1\text{ in the LP relaxation.}
G=K_n\text{ with }n\ge2\text{ for the failure boundary.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \alpha(G)=\max\left\{\sum_{v\in V}x_v:x_u+x_v\le1\ (\{u,v\}\in E),\ x\in\{0,1\}^{V}\right\},\qquad z_{LP}(G)\ge |V|/2;\qquad \alpha(K_n)=1,\ z_{LP}(K_n)\ge n/2.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Minimum-weight vertex cover and complementary independent set
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines weighted vertex cover, its binary formulation and LP relaxation, and its complementarity with maximum-weight independent set; the complexity claim concerns the decision problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an undirected graph $G=(V,E)$ with positive vertex weights $w_j$, a vertex cover is a set $C\subseteq V$ containing at least one endpoint of every edge, and minimum-weight vertex cover is $\min\{\sum_{j\in V}w_jx_j:x_i+x_j\geq1\ \forall\{i,j\}\in E,\ x_j\in\{0,1\}\}$. knowledge_statements.statement_title: Weighted Vertex-Cover Formulation and Half-Integral Feasible Solutions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the integer formulation, its LP relaxation, and half-integrality for minimum-weight vertex cover.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a graph $G=(V,E)$ and nonnegative weights $c:V\to\mathbb{Q}_{\ge 0}$, minimum-weight vertex cover has the integer formulation $\min\{\sum_{v\in V}c(v)x_v:x_u+x_v\ge1\ \forall\{u,v\}\in E,\ x_v\in\{0,1\}\ \forall v\in V\}$. Its LP relaxation replaces $x_v\in\{0,1\}$ with $x_v\ge0$. A feasible solution of the relaxation is half-integral if $x_v\in\{0,\tfrac12,1\}$ for every $v\in V$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Minimum-weight vertex cover minimizes the total weight of selected vertices while requiring at least one endpoint of every edge to be selected. Its LP relaxation uses nonnegative variables, and a feasible relaxed solution is half-integral when every coordinate is 0, 1/2, or 1.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x\text{ is half-integral}\iff x\text{ is feasible for the relaxation and }x_v\in\{0,\tfrac12,1\}\ \forall v\in V

children.title: Weighted Cover Regime Transfers
children.top_down_role: Structural relationships between cardinality-based and weighted cover instances.

knowledge_statements.title: Weighted Cover Regime Transfers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Integer vertex costs reduce to cardinality cover through independent modules.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,E)\) and \(w:V\to\mathbb{Z}_{>0}\). Replace each \(v\) by an independent set \(I_v\) of \(w(v)\) copies, and replace every edge \(uv\) by all edges between \(I_u\) and \(I_v\), obtaining \(G^w\). Then
\[\tau(G^w)=\tau_w(G).\]
There is an optimal cover of \(G^w\) containing either all or none of each \(I_v\); its selected modules project to a vertex cover of \(G\), and every cover of \(G\) lifts with equal cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Positive integer vertex costs can be encoded by independent modules, preserving minimum cover value and allowing optimal solutions to transfer both ways.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\tau(G^w)=\tau_w(G)\), with cost-preserving lifting and projection of optimal covers.

notation.meaning: the independent module replacing vertex v

children.title: Partial Vertex Cover
children.top_down_role: Vertex-cover variants permitting incomplete edge coverage.

knowledge_statements.title: Partial Vertex Cover
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimum-cost selection required to cover a prescribed edge weight.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,E)\), let \(c:V\to\mathbb{R}_{\ge0}\), let \(p:E\to\mathbb{R}_{\ge0}\), and let \(K\ge0\). For \(S\subseteq V\), define \(E(S)=\{uv\in E:u\in S\text{ or }v\in S\}\). The partial vertex-cover problem is
\[\min_{S\subseteq V}\left\{\sum_{v\in S}c(v):\sum_{e\in E(S)}p(e)\ge K\right\}.\]
The instance is feasible exactly when \(K\le\sum_{e\in E}p(e)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Select minimum-cost vertices whose incident edges have total covered weight at least a prescribed target.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{PVC}(G,c,p,K)=\min\{c(S):S\subseteq V,\ p(E(S))\ge K\}\).

notation.meaning: edges having at least one endpoint in S

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Partial vertex cover has multiple formulations, and no source establishes that this weighted target formulation is the intended local sense. The conclusion also uses c(S) and p(E(S)) without defining those aggregate abbreviations.

children.title: Budgeted Vertex Cover
children.top_down_role: Vertex-cover variants constrained by a selection budget.

knowledge_statements.title: Budgeted Vertex Cover
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Maximum edge coverage subject to a vertex-cost budget.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,E)\), let \(c:V\to\mathbb{R}_{\ge0}\), let \(p:E\to\mathbb{R}_{\ge0}\), and let \(B\ge0\). With \(E(S)=\{uv\in E:u\in S\text{ or }v\in S\}\), the budgeted vertex-cover problem is
\[\max_{S\subseteq V}\left\{\sum_{e\in E(S)}p(e):\sum_{v\in S}c(v)\le B\right\}.\]
Each edge is counted once even when both endpoints belong to \(S\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under a vertex-cost budget, select vertices maximizing the total weight of edges incident to at least one selected vertex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{BVC}(G,c,p,B)=\max\{p(E(S)):S\subseteq V,\ c(S)\le B\}\).

notation.meaning: edges covered by the selected vertices
maximum covered-edge weight under the budget

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No citation establishes this weighted maximum-coverage formulation as the intended meaning of budgeted vertex cover. The conclusion additionally uses c(S) and p(E(S)) without defining those aggregate abbreviations.

children.title: Coverage–Cost Tradeoff Regimes
children.top_down_role: Objective and feasibility regimes linking coverage targets to resource limits.

knowledge_statements.title: Coverage–Cost Tradeoff Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bicriteria formulation unifying partial and budgeted weighted vertex cover.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let vertex costs and edge profits be nonnegative. For \(S\subseteq V\), define \(c(S)=\sum_{v\in S}c_v\) and \(p(S)=\sum_{e\in E:e\cap S\ne\varnothing}p_e\). For \(B,Q\in\mathbb R_+\), define
\[F(B)=\max\{p(S):S\subseteq V,\ c(S)\le B\},\qquad K(Q)=\min\{c(S):S\subseteq V,\ p(S)\ge Q\}.\]
With an infeasible minimum interpreted as \(+\infty\), \(K(Q)\le B\) if and only if \(F(B)\ge Q\). Thus either value function determines the attainable coverage–cost frontier.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For nonnegative B and Q, minimum cost for coverage Q is at most B exactly when maximum coverage under budget B is at least Q.
assumptions_latex: \(c_v\ge0\) for every \(v\in V\), and \(p_e\ge0\) for every \(e\in E\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K(Q)\le B\iff F(B)\ge Q\).

notation.meaning: maximum covered edge profit under vertex-cost budget B
minimum vertex cost attaining edge profit at least Q

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: direct equivalence of the standard partial and budgeted vertex-cover formulations

knowledge_statements.title: Clique–Stable-Set Complementation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Set-system and optimum-value correspondence under graph complementation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(S\subseteq V\), the set \(S\) is stable in \(G\) if and only if every two distinct vertices of \(S\) are adjacent in the complement \(\overline G\), equivalently, \(S\) is a clique of \(\overline G\). Hence the stable sets of \(G\) and cliques of \(\overline G\) are identical as vertex subsets, and
\[\alpha(G)=\omega(\overline G),\qquad \omega(G)=\alpha(\overline G).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A vertex set is stable in a graph exactly when it is a clique in the complement; the corresponding optimum cardinalities agree.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite simple undirected graph.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(S\subseteq V\), \(S\) is stable in \(G\) if and only if \(S\) is a clique in \(\overline G\); moreover, \(\alpha(G)=\omega(\overline G)\) and \(\omega(G)=\alpha(\overline G)\).

notation.meaning: complement of G on the same vertex set

knowledge_statements.title: Stable-Set–Vertex-Cover Complementation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Complementation within the common vertex set, including nonnegative vertex weights.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(S\subseteq V\), the set \(S\) is stable in \(G\) if and only if \(V\setminus S\) is a vertex cover of \(G\). Consequently, complementation is a bijection between stable sets and vertex covers. For nonnegative vertex weights \(w\),
\[\tau_w(G)=w(V)-\alpha_w(G),\]
where \(w(V)=\sum_{v\in V}w_v\), \(\tau_w(G)\) is the minimum weight of a vertex cover, and \(\alpha_w(G)\) is the maximum weight of a stable set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The complement of a stable set is a vertex cover and conversely; minimum cover weight equals total weight minus maximum stable-set weight.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S\text{ stable}\iff V\setminus S\text{ is a vertex cover}\), and \(\tau_w(G)=w(V)-\alpha_w(G)\).

notation.meaning: minimum weight of a vertex cover
maximum weight of a stable set

knowledge_statements.title: Line-Graph Matching Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Matching problems represented as stable-set problems on line graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The line graph \(L(G)\) has vertex set \(E(G)\), with two vertices adjacent exactly when their corresponding edges share an endpoint in \(G\). Therefore \(M\subseteq E(G)\) is a matching in \(G\) if and only if the corresponding vertex subset is stable in \(L(G)\). This bijection preserves cardinality and edge weights, so
\[\nu(G)=\alpha(L(G))\quad\text{and}\quad \nu_w(G)=\alpha_w(L(G)).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Edges form a matching in G exactly when their corresponding vertices form a stable set in the line graph, preserving size and weight.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is a finite loopless undirected graph.
\(w:E(G)\to\mathbb R\) assigns the same weight to each edge and its line-graph vertex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M\text{ is a matching in }G\iff M\text{ is stable in }L(G)\), and \(\nu_w(G)=\alpha_w(L(G))\).

notation.meaning: maximum weight of a matching in G

children.title: Edge Inequality Families

knowledge_statements.title: Edge Inequality Families
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Basic linear relaxation constraints for incidence vectors of stable sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Every incidence vector \(x\) of a stable set satisfies
\[x_u+x_v\le1\qquad\text{for every }uv\in E.\]
Together with \(0\le x_v\le1\) for all \(v\in V\), these constraints define the edge relaxation
\[Q_{\mathrm{edge}}(G)=\{x\in[0,1]^V:x_u+x_v\le1\text{ for every }uv\in E\},\]
which contains the stable-set polytope \(\operatorname{STAB}(G)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A stable set cannot contain both endpoints of an edge; the resulting edge relaxation contains the stable-set polytope.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{STAB}(G)\subseteq Q_{\mathrm{edge}}(G)\).

notation.meaning: convex hull of stable-set incidence vectors

children.title: Clique Inequality Families

knowledge_statements.title: Clique Inequality Families
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Clique constraints for the stable-set polytope and its clique relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every nonempty clique \(K\) of \(G\), any stable-set incidence vector \(x\) satisfies
\[\sum_{v\in K}x_v\le1.\]
The clique relaxation is
\[Q_{\mathrm{clq}}(G)=\left\{x\in\mathbb R_{+}^{V}:\sum_{v\in K}x_v\le1\text{ for every clique }K\right\}.\]
Every stable-set incidence vector belongs to this relaxation, and therefore \(\operatorname{STAB}(G)\subseteq Q_{\mathrm{clq}}(G)\). Singleton cliques supply the upper bounds \(x_v\le1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At most one vertex of any clique can belong to a stable set; all such inequalities define the clique relaxation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{STAB}(G)\subseteq Q_{\mathrm{clq}}(G)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Clique Inequalities for the Stable-Set Polytope
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the source's convention that a clique is an inclusion-wise maximal complete subgraph and records validity and dominance properties of its inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: \forall\mathbf{x}\in\operatorname{VP}(G),\quad \sum_{i\in V(K)}x_i\le 1\quad\text{for every clique }K.\qquad \left[\mathbf{x}\ge0\ \land\ \sum_{i\in V(K)}x_i\le1\ \forall K\right]\Longrightarrow x_i+x_j\le1\quad\forall ij\in E(G).

Every stable-set-polytope vector has coordinate sum at most one on each clique. For nonnegative vectors, these clique inequalities imply all edge inequalities, and the inequality for a nonmaximal complete subgraph follows from that of a containing clique.

children.title: Edge-to-Clique Dominance Relations
children.top_down_role: Strength and redundancy relationships between the two inequality families.

knowledge_statements.title: Edge-to-Clique Dominance Relations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strict relaxation dominance of clique inequalities over edge inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Under nonnegativity, each clique inequality \(\sum_{v\in K}x_v\le1\) implies every edge inequality \(x_u+x_v\le1\) with \(u,v\in K\). Hence
\[Q_{\mathrm{clq}}(G)\subseteq Q_{\mathrm{edge}}(G).\]
The inclusion is strict whenever \(G\) has a clique \(K\) with \(|K|\ge3\): assigning \(x_v=1/2\) on \(K\) and \(x_v=0\) elsewhere satisfies every edge inequality but violates the clique inequality for \(K\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Clique inequalities imply their constituent edge inequalities and are strictly stronger when the graph contains a clique of size at least three.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Q_{\mathrm{clq}}(G)\subseteq Q_{\mathrm{edge}}(G)\), strictly if \(\omega(G)\ge3\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: immediate polyhedral dominance between classical stable-set relaxations
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The dominance and strictness claim is correct for the defined relaxations, but it has no inspectable citation.

children.title: Odd-Cycle Inequality Families

knowledge_statements.title: Odd-Cycle Inequality Families
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Valid stable-set inequalities indexed by simple odd cycles.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\) be a simple odd cycle of length \(|V(C)|=2k+1\) in \(G\). Every stable set contains at most \(k\) vertices of \(C\); hence its incidence vector satisfies the odd-cycle inequality
\[\sum_{v\in V(C)}x_v\le k=\left\lfloor\frac{|V(C)|}{2}\right\rfloor.\]
The inequality remains valid when \(C\) has chords, although additional edges may make it redundant or dominated by stronger inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every odd cycle of length 2k+1 contributes a valid inequality limiting a stable set to at most k cycle vertices.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a simple cycle of odd length \(2k+1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sum_{v\in V(C)}x_v\le k\) is valid for \(\operatorname{STAB}(G)\).

notation.meaning: a simple odd cycle in G
integer satisfying the cycle length equation \(2k+1\)

children.title: Odd-Hole Inequality Families

knowledge_statements.title: Odd-Hole Inequality Families
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Odd-cycle inequalities restricted to chordless cycles of length at least five.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
An odd hole is an induced cycle \(H\cong C_{2k+1}\) with \(k\ge2\). Since \(\alpha(H)=k\), every point of \(\operatorname{STAB}(G)\) satisfies
\[\sum_{v\in V(H)}x_v\le k.\]
For the induced subgraph \(H\) itself, this inequality defines a facet of \(\operatorname{STAB}(H)\). In the ambient graph it is a valid induced-subgraph inequality, though facetness may require lifting or additional hypotheses.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each induced odd cycle of length at least five yields a rank inequality, facet-defining for the stable-set polytope of that cycle.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sum_{v\in U}x_v\le k\) is valid for \(\operatorname{STAB}(G)\) and facet-defining for \(\operatorname{STAB}(H)\).

notation.meaning: an induced odd cycle, or odd hole
vertex set of the odd hole

children.title: Induced-Cycle Strengthening Regimes
children.top_down_role: Strength, redundancy, and applicability contrasts between cycle-based families.

knowledge_statements.title: Induced-Cycle Strengthening Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Parity criterion for strengthening the edge relaxation on chordless cycles.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H=G[U]\) be an induced cycle. If \(|U|=2k\), summing its \(2k\) edge inequalities and dividing by two gives \(\sum_{v\in U}x_v\le k\), so the cycle-rank bound is already implied by the edge relaxation. If \(|U|=2k+1\), the edge inequalities imply only \(\sum_{v\in U}x_v\le k+1/2\); the point given by \(x_v=1/2\) for \(v\in U\) and \(x_v=0\) for \(v\notin U\) demonstrates that the strengthened valid inequality \(\sum_{v\in U}x_v\le k\) is not implied by the edge relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Even-cycle rank bounds follow from edge constraints, whereas odd induced cycles require a strictly stronger integral rank inequality.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(|U|\) is even, the cycle-rank inequality is implied by the edge relaxation; if \(|U|\) is odd, \(\sum_{v\in U}x_v\le\lfloor |U|/2\rfloor\) is a strict strengthening of that relaxation.

notation.meaning: edge-inequality relaxation of the stable-set polytope
vertex set of the induced cycle

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: parity consequence obtained by summing cycle edge inequalities

children.title: Rank Inequality Families

knowledge_statements.title: Rank Inequality Families
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Induced-subgraph rank inequalities for the stable-set polytope.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every nonempty vertex subset \(U\subseteq V\), define its rank as the stability number \(\alpha(G[U])\). Every stable-set incidence vector satisfies
\[\sum_{v\in U}x_v\le\alpha(G[U]).\]
These are the rank inequalities of \(G\). They specialize to clique inequalities when \(\alpha(G[U])=1\) and to odd-hole inequalities when \(G[U]\cong C_{2k+1}\), for which the right-hand side is \(k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every induced subgraph bounds the number of selected vertices by its stability number, subsuming clique and odd-hole inequalities.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sum_{v\in U}x_v\le\alpha(G[U])\) is valid for \(\operatorname{STAB}(G)\).

notation.meaning: subgraph of G induced by U
maximum cardinality of a stable set in the induced subgraph

children.title: Lifted Inequality Families

knowledge_statements.title: Lifted Inequality Families
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential lifting of a valid face inequality for a binary polytope.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\subseteq\{0,1\}^{I\cup J}\), and suppose \(a^{\mathsf T}x_I\le b\) is valid when \(x_J=0\). Order \(J=(j_1,\ldots,j_m)\). At step \(t\), keep \(x_{j_s}=0\) for \(s>t\) and set
\[\lambda_{j_t}=b-\max\left\{a^{\mathsf T}x_I+\sum_{s<t}\lambda_{j_s}x_{j_s}:x\in X,\ x_{j_t}=1,\ x_{j_s}=0\text{ for }s>t\right\}.\]
After all steps, output \(a^{\mathsf T}x_I+\sum_{j\in J}\lambda_jx_j\le b\), which is valid for \(\operatorname{conv}(X)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sequential lifting computes coefficients for formerly fixed binary variables, extending a valid face inequality to the full binary polytope.
assumptions_latex: \(a^{\mathsf T}x_I\le b\) is valid on \(\{x\in X:x_J=0\}\).
Each maximization slice used by the lifting order is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(a^{\mathsf T}x_I+\sum_{j\in J}\lambda_jx_j\le b\) is valid for \(\operatorname{conv}(X)\).

notation.meaning: indices present in the initial face inequality

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard sequential up-lifting construction for binary polytopes
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

children.title: Rank-to-Lifting Strength Relations
children.top_down_role: Connections between base rank inequalities and their lifted extensions.

knowledge_statements.title: Rank-to-Lifting Strength Relations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential lifting of a valid rank inequality from an induced subgraph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(U\subseteq V(G)\), and suppose \(a^\top x\leq \beta\) is valid for \(\operatorname{STAB}(G[U])\). Order \(V(G)\setminus U=\{v_1,\ldots,v_k\}\). At step \(i\), after coefficients for \(v_1,\ldots,v_{i-1}\) have been fixed, set \[a_{v_i}:=\beta-\max\left\{\sum_{u\in U\cup\{v_1,\ldots,v_{i-1}\}}a_u x_u:x\in\operatorname{STAB}(G[U\cup\{v_1,\ldots,v_i\}]),\ x_{v_i}=1\right\}.\] The resulting lifted inequality is valid for \(\operatorname{STAB}(G)\) and restricts to the original rank inequality on the face \(x_{V(G)\setminus U}=0\). Its coefficients, and thus its global strength, may depend on the lifting order.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sequential lifting preserves validity and the original inequality on its induced-subgraph face, but different lifting orders can produce different global inequalities.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sum_{v\in V(G)}a_vx_v\leq\beta\) is valid for \(\operatorname{STAB}(G)\).

notation.meaning: convex hull of incidence vectors of stable sets of G

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The sequential lifting statement is mathematically plausible and fits the property container, but no inspectable source supports the coefficient formula or order-dependence claim.

children.title: Stable-Set Polytope Facets
children.top_down_role: Facet classes and structural conditions within stable-set polytope geometry.

knowledge_statements.title: Stable-Set Polytope Facets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear-algebraic criterion for a valid inequality to define a facet.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) have \(n=|V|\), and let \(P=\operatorname{STAB}(G)\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{V}\). Because \(0\) and every unit vector belong to \(P\), the polytope is full-dimensional. A nonzero valid inequality \(a^\top x\leq\beta\) defines a facet of \(P\) if and only if its tight face \[F=\{x\in P:a^\top x=\beta\}\] has dimension \(n-1\). Equivalently, there exist \(n\) affinely independent stable-set incidence vectors \(\chi^{S_1},\ldots,\chi^{S_n}\) satisfying \(a^\top\chi^{S_i}=\beta\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A valid stable-set inequality is facet-defining exactly when its tight stable-set vectors contain n affinely independent points.
assumptions_latex: \(a^\top x\leq\beta\) is a nonzero valid inequality for \(\operatorname{STAB}(G)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(a^\top x\leq\beta\) defines a facet if and only if \(\dim(F)=|V|-1\).

notation.meaning: incidence vector of the stable set S
face on which the inequality is tight

children.title: Stable-Set Polytope Adjacency
children.top_down_role: Adjacency structure among vertices or faces of the stable-set polytope.

knowledge_statements.title: Stable-Set Polytope Adjacency
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Combinatorial characterization of adjacency between stable-set vertices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\) and \(T\) be distinct stable sets of a finite simple graph \(G\). Their incidence vectors \(\chi^S\) and \(\chi^T\) are adjacent vertices of \(\operatorname{STAB}(G)\) if and only if the subgraph induced by their symmetric difference, \(G[S\triangle T]\), is connected. Thus adjacency of two stable-set vertices can be tested solely on the vertices selected by exactly one of the two stable sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two stable-set vertices are adjacent precisely when the graph induced by the symmetric difference of their stable sets is connected.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\chi^S\) and \(\chi^T\) are adjacent in \(\operatorname{STAB}(G)\) if and only if \(G[S\triangle T]\) is connected.

notation.meaning: symmetric difference of S and T

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The symmetric-difference connectivity characterization matches the theorem container and is stated consistently, but this nontrivial characterization requires an inspectable theorem or section citation.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Adjacency Criterion for Stable-Set Incidence Vectors
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Vertex adjacency characterized by connectivity of the subgraph induced by the symmetric difference.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\), and let \(R\ne S\) be stable sets of \(G\). The vertices \(\mathbf1_R\) and \(\mathbf1_S\) of \(P_{\mathrm{stable}}(G)\) are adjacent if and only if \(G[R\triangle S]\) is connected.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The incidence vectors of two distinct stable sets are adjacent in the stable-set polytope exactly when their symmetric difference induces a connected subgraph.
assumptions_latex: R,S\subseteq V\text{ are distinct stable sets of }G
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathbf1_R\text{ and }\mathbf1_S\text{ are adjacent in }P_{\mathrm{stable}}(G)\iff G[R\triangle S]\text{ is connected}

children.title: Facet–Adjacency Relations
children.top_down_role: Geometric links between facet incidence and adjacency structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Facet–Adjacency Relations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ridge-incidence criterion for adjacency of stable-set-polytope facets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P=\operatorname{STAB}(G)\) have dimension \(d=|V(G)|\), and let \(F_1\) and \(F_2\) be distinct facets of \(P\). The facets are adjacent in the facet-adjacency graph exactly when their intersection is a ridge of \(P\): \[F_1\sim F_2\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \dim(F_1\cap F_2)=d-2.\] Equivalently, the two corresponding vertices of the polar polytope are joined by an edge whenever a polar representation is taken with the origin in the interior.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two facets are adjacent exactly when they meet in a codimension-two face; under polarity, their corresponding polar vertices are adjacent.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F_1\sim F_2\) if and only if \(\dim(F_1\cap F_2)=|V(G)|-2\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The ridge criterion and qualified polarity statement are mathematically appropriate for this condition container, but no supporting polyhedral reference is supplied.

knowledge_statements.title: Fractional Stable-Set Relaxations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Box-bounded edge relaxation paired with the standard fractional vertex-cover formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite simple graph \(G=(V,E)\) and weights \(w\in\mathbb{R}_{+}^{V}\), define the edge-based fractional stable-set polytope by \[\operatorname{FRAC}(G)=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^{V}:0\leq x_v\leq1\ (v\in V),\ x_u+x_v\leq1\ (uv\in E)\}.\] The fractional stable-set relaxation is \(\max\{w^\top x:x\in\operatorname{FRAC}(G)\}\). Every stable-set incidence vector is feasible, so \(\operatorname{STAB}(G)\subseteq\operatorname{FRAC}(G)\); consequently, the relaxation optimum is an upper bound on the maximum-weight stable-set value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The box-bounded edge relaxation imposes one inequality per edge, contains the stable-set polytope, and upper-bounds the maximum-weight stable-set value.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{STAB}(G)\subseteq\operatorname{FRAC}(G)\) and \(\alpha_w(G)\leq\max_{x\in\operatorname{FRAC}(G)}w^\top x\).

notation.meaning: maximum weight of a stable set

children.title: Fractional Vertex-Cover Relaxation
children.top_down_role: Fractional vertex-cover optimization and its polyhedral structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Fractional Vertex-Cover Relaxation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard linear relaxation of minimum-weight vertex cover.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite simple graph \(G=(V,E)\) with costs \(c\in\mathbb{R}_{+}^{V}\), the fractional vertex-cover relaxation is \[\tau_f(G,c)=\min\left\{\sum_{v\in V}c_vy_v:y_u+y_v\geq1\ (uv\in E),\ y_v\geq0\ (v\in V)\right\}.\] Bounds \(y_v\leq1\) may be added without changing the optimum. Every vertex-cover incidence vector is feasible, hence \(\tau_f(G,c)\leq\tau(G,c)\). Under the substitution \(x_v=1-y_v\), its feasible region with box bounds is complementary to the edge-based fractional stable-set relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fractional vertex cover replaces binary choices by nonnegative variables covering every edge; its optimum lower-bounds integral vertex cover.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\tau_f(G,c)\leq\tau(G,c)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Fractional vertex covers and their matching dual
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines fractional vertex covers and fractional matchings and records the complement relation, optimum-value identities, and half-integrality of the fractional matching polytope.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a graph \(G=(V,E)\), a fractional vertex cover is a vector \(x\in\mathbb R^V\) such that \(0\le x_v\le1\) for every \(v\in V\) and \(x_u+x_v\ge1\) for every \(\{u,v\}\in E\). A vector \(x\) is a fractional vertex cover if and only if \(\mathbf1-x\) is a fractional stable set; consequently, \(\tau^*(G)+\alpha^*(G)=|V|\). Moreover, \(\tau^*(G)=\nu^*(G)\), where \(\nu^*(G)=\max\{y(E):0\le y_e\le1\ (e\in E),\ y(\delta(v))\le1\ (v\in V)\}\). Every vertex of the fractional matching polytope is half-integral.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fractional vertex cover assigns values between zero and one to the vertices so that the endpoints of every edge have total value at least one. Complementing it gives a fractional stable set, so their optimum values sum to the number of vertices. Linear-programming duality equates the fractional vertex-cover number with the fractional matching number. Every extreme point of the fractional matching polytope is half-integral.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \tau^*(G)+\alpha^*(G)=|V|,\qquad \tau^*(G)=\nu^*(G),\qquad \operatorname{vert}(P_{FM}(G))\subseteq\{0,\tfrac12,1\}^E.

children.title: Fractional Matching Dual
children.top_down_role: The matching-side optimization object paired with fractional vertex cover.

knowledge_statements.title: Fractional Matching Dual
knowledge_statements.scope_note: LP dual of the fractional vertex-cover relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The linear-programming dual of the fractional vertex-cover relaxation is \[\nu_f(G,c)=\max\left\{\sum_{e\in E}z_e:z_e\geq0\ (e\in E),\ \sum_{e\in\delta(v)}z_e\leq c_v\ (v\in V)\right\}.\] A feasible vector \(z\) is a fractional matching with vertex capacities \(c\). Since both programs are feasible and have finite optima, strong linear-programming duality gives \(\nu_f(G,c)=\tau_f(G,c)\). For unit costs, each vertex is incident to total matching weight at most one.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The dual packs nonnegative edge weights subject to vertex capacities, and its optimum equals the fractional vertex-cover optimum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\nu_f(G,c)=\tau_f(G,c)\).

notation.meaning: set of edges incident with v

knowledge_statements.title: Vertex-Cover–Matching Duality Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fractional equality generally and integral equality for bipartite graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every finite graph \(G\) with unit vertex costs, strong linear-programming duality yields \(	au_f(G)=
u_f(G)\). If \(G\) is bipartite, the vertex-edge incidence system is totally dual integral, so integral optima exist and \[	au(G)=	au_f(G)=
u_f(G)=
u(G),\] which is König's vertex-cover–matching theorem. For nonbipartite graphs the fractional equality remains valid, but integral equality can fail; for example, on an odd cycle \(C_{2k+1}\), \(	au(C_{2k+1})=k+1\) while \(
u(C_{2k+1})=k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fractional cover and matching values always agree. Integral equality holds for bipartite graphs but can fail on odd cycles.

children.title: Half-Integral Extreme Points
children.top_down_role: Polyhedral regimes exhibiting half-integral relaxation structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Half-Integral Extreme Points
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Half-integrality of the standard vertex-cover linear relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \[P_{VC}(G)=\{y\in\mathbb{R}^{V}:y_u+y_v\geq1\ (uv\in E),\ y_v\geq0\ (v\in V)\}.\] Every extreme point \(y\) of \(P_{VC}(G)\) is half-integral: \[y_v\in\left\{0,\tfrac12,1\right\}\qquad(v\in V).\] Consequently, for every nonnegative cost vector, the fractional vertex-cover program has an optimal solution whose coordinates belong to \(\{0,\tfrac12,1\}\). Under the complementary substitution \(x_v=1-y_v\) with box bounds, the corresponding extreme solutions of the edge stable-set relaxation are likewise half-integral.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every extreme solution of the vertex-cover LP uses only 0, one-half, and 1; an optimal half-integral solution therefore always exists.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{ext}(P_{VC}(G))\subseteq\{0,\tfrac12,1\}^{V}\).

notation.meaning: set of extreme points of P

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The half-integrality theorem and its optimal-solution consequence are correctly scoped, but this nontrivial theorem requires an authoritative citation with a specific locator.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Half-Integrality of Vertex-Cover LP Extreme Points
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The extreme-point structure of the standard vertex-cover LP relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $P=\{x\in\mathbb{R}_{\ge0}^{V}:x_u+x_v\ge1\ \text{for every }\{u,v\}\in E\}$. Every extreme point $x$ of $P$ is half-integral; that is, $x_v\in\{0,\tfrac12,1\}$ for every $v\in V$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every extreme point of the standard vertex-cover LP relaxation has each coordinate equal to 0, 1/2, or 1.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x_v\in\{0,\tfrac12,1\}\quad\forall v\in V

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Non-Half-Integral Vertex-Cover LP Solutions Are Not Extreme
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A nonextremality criterion for feasible solutions of the standard vertex-cover LP relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $P=\{x\in\mathbb{R}_{\ge0}^{V}:x_u+x_v\ge1\ \text{for every }\{u,v\}\in E\}$. If $x\in P$ is not half-integral, then $x$ is a convex combination of two distinct feasible points of $P$ and hence is not an extreme point of $P$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every feasible solution of the standard vertex-cover LP that is not half-integral is a nontrivial convex combination of two distinct feasible solutions and therefore is not an extreme point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists y,z\in P,\ y\ne z,\ \exists\lambda\in(0,1):x=\lambda y+(1-\lambda)z;\quad x\notin\operatorname{ext}(P)
