children.title: Meyniel–Orderability Relations
children.top_down_role: Inclusion, overlap, and separation between Meyniel graphs and perfectly orderable graphs.

assumptions_latex: Every odd cycle of \(G\) of length at least five has at least two chords.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G\) is perfectly orderable and hence perfect.

notation.meaning: Chromatic and clique numbers of a graph

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the finite simple-graph form of the Meyniel-to-perfect-orderability inclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A graph satisfying the stated odd-cycle condition is a Meyniel graph. There exists a vertex ordering \(v_1,\ldots,v_n\) such that, for every induced subgraph \(H\) of \(G\), greedy coloring of \(H\) in the restricted ordering uses exactly \(\omega(H)\) colors. Consequently, every induced subgraph satisfies \(\chi(H)=\omega(H)\), so \(G\) is perfect. Thus the class of Meyniel graphs is contained in the class of perfectly orderable graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every Meyniel graph has an ordering under which greedy coloring is optimal on every induced subgraph; consequently every Meyniel graph is perfect.
knowledge_statements.title: Meyniel–Orderability Relations

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem fits the relations leaf, but the Meyniel-to-perfect-orderability inclusion and the direction of the greedy ordering require a specialized source with a precise theorem locator.

children.title: Zero-Joins
children.top_down_role: Disconnected decomposition structure and its role in graph reconstruction.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((X_1,X_2)\) is a zero-join exactly when \(E(X_1,X_2)=\varnothing\).

notation.meaning: Edges having one endpoint in each displayed set
The two sides of the partition

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the standard nontrivial vertex-partition convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A zero-join of \(G\) is a partition \(V=X_1\mathbin{\dot\cup}X_2\) such that \(X_1\neq\varnothing\), \(X_2\neq\varnothing\), and no edge has one endpoint in each side. Equivalently, \(E(X_1,X_2)=\varnothing\). Hence \(G[X_1]\) and \(G[X_2]\) are unions of distinct connected components of \(G\); in particular, \(G\) admits a zero-join if and only if it is disconnected.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A zero-join is a nontrivial partition with no edge between its two sides; it exists exactly when the graph is disconnected.
knowledge_statements.title: Zero-Joins

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition is mathematically plausible and fits the leaf, but no source establishes the nonempty-side convention or the claimed equivalence with disconnectedness under that convention.

children.title: One-Joins
children.top_down_role: One-join separation structure, admissible graph regimes, and decomposition boundaries.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The cross-edge set is exactly \(E(X_1,X_2)=A_1\times A_2\).

notation.meaning: The sides of the vertex partition

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the cross-edge characterization; side-size conventions vary between decomposition sources.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A one-join of \(G\) consists of a partition \(V=X_1\mathbin{\dot\cup}X_2\), with \(X_1,X_2\neq\varnothing\), and nonempty sets \(A_i\subseteq X_i\) for \(i\in\{1,2\}\), such that every vertex of \(A_1\) is adjacent to every vertex of \(A_2\), and there are no other edges between \(X_1\) and \(X_2\). Equivalently, the bipartite graph of cross edges is the single complete bipartite graph with parts \(A_1,A_2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A one-join partitions the vertices so that all cross edges, and only those edges, form one complete bipartite attachment.
knowledge_statements.title: One-Joins

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The cross-edge description fits a one-join definition, but one-join conventions differ on side sizes and whether attachment sets must be proper. A specialized source is required before fixing the definition.

children.title: Two-Joins
children.top_down_role: Two-join structure, principal variants, and its role in Berge-graph decomposition.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(E(X_1,X_2)=(A_1\times A_2)\mathbin{\dot\cup}(B_1\times B_2)\).

notation.meaning: The two sides of the split
The two attachment sets on side i

knowledge_statements.scope_note: States the core two-join; connectedness and path-side exclusions are additional variants.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A two-join of \(G\) is a partition \(V=X_1\mathbin{\dot\cup}X_2\), where \(|X_i|\geq 3\), together with pairwise disjoint nonempty sets \(A_i,B_i\subseteq X_i\) for \(i\in\{1,2\}\). Every vertex of \(A_1\) is adjacent to every vertex of \(A_2\), every vertex of \(B_1\) is adjacent to every vertex of \(B_2\), and no other edge joins \(X_1\) to \(X_2\). The sets \(C_i=X_i\setminus(A_i\cup B_i)\) may be empty.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A two-join has two disjoint complete attachment pairs across a vertex partition and no other cross edges.
knowledge_statements.title: Two-Joins

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record gives a common core of a two-join, but standard variants differ regarding connectedness and exclusion of path sides. The exact definition for this decomposition taxonomy requires a cited source.

children.title: Join-Type Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Distinctions, overlaps, and exceptional regimes across zero-, one-, and two-joins.

assumptions_latex: All join types use nonempty partition sides and exact cross-edge specifications.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Zero-, one-, and two-joins are distinguished by zero, one, and two nonempty complete-bipartite cross-edge components, subject to their respective side conditions.

notation.meaning: The bipartite graph consisting of edges crossing the partition

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates join arities by the exact structure of the cross-edge bipartite graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a fixed partition \(V=X_1\mathbin{\dot\cup}X_2\), a zero-join has no cross edge, a one-join has cross-edge graph equal to one nonempty complete bipartite graph, and a two-join has cross-edge graph equal to the disjoint union of two nonempty complete bipartite graphs with disjoint attachment sets. A cross-edge graph with three such components, or with a component that is not complete bipartite, satisfies none of these definitions. Degenerate empty attachment sets collapse arity and must therefore be excluded.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Join arity counts disjoint complete-bipartite cross attachments; extra, incomplete, or empty attachments place a partition outside or below the stated type.
knowledge_statements.title: Join-Type Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The boundary discussion depends on the precise zero-, one-, and two-join conventions. In particular, side restrictions and excluded two-join degeneracies must be established before the stated cross-edge classification is reliable.

children.title: Clique Cutsets
children.top_down_role: Separator-based decomposition structure centered on clique cutsets.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K\) is a clique cutset exactly when \(G[K]\) is complete and \(G-K\) is disconnected.

notation.meaning: The graph obtained by deleting K and its incident edges

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses vertex cutsets; the empty set is allowed only when explicitly treating disconnected graphs.

source_refs.locator: 0.2 Graph Theory p. 16

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A clique cutset of \(G\) is a proper vertex subset \(K\subsetneq V\) such that every two distinct vertices of \(K\) are adjacent and \(G-K\) has at least two connected components. Equivalently, there exist nonempty disjoint sets \(X_1,X_2\) with \(V=K\mathbin{\dot\cup}X_1\mathbin{\dot\cup}X_2\) and no edge between \(X_1\) and \(X_2\). A clique-cutset decomposition replaces \(G\) by the induced blocks \(G[K\cup X_1]\) and \(G[K\cup X_2]\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A clique cutset is a clique whose deletion disconnects the graph; decomposition blocks retain the cutset with each separated side.
knowledge_statements.title: Clique Cutsets

source_witnesses.locator: 0.2 Graph Theory p. 16

children.title: Amalgam Decompositions
children.top_down_role: Amalgam structure, decomposition scope, and relevant graph-class regimes.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The partition \((V_1,A_1,K,A_2,V_2)\) defines an amalgam split of \(G\).

notation.meaning: Complete attachment sets on the two sides
Interior sets on the two sides

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the five-part perfect-graph amalgam convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An amalgam split is a partition \(V=V_1\mathbin{\dot\cup}A_1\mathbin{\dot\cup}K\mathbin{\dot\cup}A_2\mathbin{\dot\cup}V_2\) in which \(A_1,A_2\neq\varnothing\), \(K\) is a clique, \(K\) is complete to \(A_1\cup A_2\), and \(A_1\) is complete to \(A_2\). There are no edges from \(V_1\) to \(V_2\cup A_2\), nor from \(V_2\) to \(V_1\cup A_1\), and each set \(V_i\cup A_i\) contains at least two vertices. The two amalgam blocks retain suitable representatives of the opposite attachment.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An amalgam split has two sides linked through complete attachment sets and a central clique, with all other cross-side edges forbidden.
knowledge_statements.title: Amalgam Decompositions

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Amalgam definitions vary in their nonemptiness and side-size conditions. Moreover, the statement mentions blocks retaining “suitable representatives” without defining them. A specialized source must fix both the split and block conventions.

children.title: Cutset–Amalgam Relations
children.top_down_role: Structural overlap, distinctions, and transfer boundaries between the two decomposition families.

assumptions_latex: Clique-cutset and amalgam decompositions use the strict definitions in their sibling records.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Neither strict decomposition notion contains the other solely by identifying its central clique with a clique cutset.

notation.meaning: The central clique of an amalgam split
The two complete attachment sets of an amalgam

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Clarifies the strict versus degenerate relationship between the two decomposition templates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In a strict amalgam, deleting the central clique \(K\) need not disconnect the graph because the nonempty sets \(A_1\) and \(A_2\) are complete to one another. Thus \(K\) need not be a clique cutset. Conversely, a clique-cutset split imposes no complete adjacency between attachment sets on opposite components, so it need not be a strict amalgam. If the amalgam template is relaxed by allowing both attachment sets to be empty, then a clique-cutset split is recovered as the degenerate case with central clique equal to the cutset.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strict amalgams and clique-cutset splits are generally incomparable; clique cutsets appear as amalgams only under a relaxed empty-attachment convention.
knowledge_statements.title: Cutset–Amalgam Relations

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The strict-case comparison is plausible, but the assertion that every clique-cutset split is recovered by merely allowing empty attachment sets may fail under retained amalgam side-size conditions. The exact convention and relation need source verification.

children.title: Decomposition-Based Recognition
children.top_down_role: Recognition frameworks organized around decomposition trees and basic graph classes.

assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal C\) is a hereditary class of finite graphs.
A finite family of valid decomposition rules and a polynomial-time basic-graph recognizer are given.
Every recursive decomposition has polynomially many nodes and polynomial-time computable splits.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The recursive procedure recognizes membership in \(\mathcal C\) in polynomial time.

notation.meaning: The decomposition tree rooted at G

knowledge_statements.scope_note: A conditional recognition interface, not a recognition theorem for all Berge graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On input \(G\), initialize a worklist with \(G\). Repeatedly remove a graph \(H\). If \(H\) is basic, apply the basic recognizer; reject if it fails. Otherwise find an applicable valid split and insert its blocks into the worklist; reject if no split exists. Accept when every leaf is accepted as basic and every internal split satisfies its rule's reconstruction equivalence. If membership of an internal graph is equivalent to membership of all its blocks, correctness follows bottom-up. Under the stated polynomial bounds, the total running time is polynomial in \(|V(G)|+|E(G)|\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Recursively split the graph, recognize basic leaves, and combine valid membership decisions; polynomial tree size and polynomial subroutines yield polynomial recognition.
knowledge_statements.title: Decomposition-Based Recognition

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits the recognition leaf, but correctness additionally depends on an explicit membership-preserving reconstruction equivalence for every split. No source or project specification establishes that interface or the complexity assumptions.

children.title: Decomposition-Based Optimization
children.top_down_role: Optimization frameworks that combine results obtained across decomposition components.

assumptions_latex: \(G\) is a finite graph with vertex weights \(w\).
A valid decomposition tree and exact leaf solvers are available.
Each split has a finite polynomial-size boundary state space with correct combination rules.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Bottom-up dynamic programming returns an optimal solution for \(G\).

notation.meaning: A decomposition-tree node representing an induced block
Optimal value in H consistent with the state

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditional dynamic-programming interface for decomposable graph optimization problems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Construct the decomposition tree and solve each leaf for every feasible boundary state \(\sigma\). Process internal nodes bottom-up. For an internal block \(H\) with children \(H_1,H_2\), compute \(F_H(\sigma)\) by optimizing the prescribed combination of \(F_{H_1}(\sigma_1)\) and \(F_{H_2}(\sigma_2)\) over compatible child states, correcting for duplicated marker or separator contributions. Store an attaining choice. At the root, output the best unrestricted state and recover a solution by backtracking. Exactness requires that every global feasible solution restrict to compatible child states and every compatible combination reconstruct a feasible global solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Solve basic leaves by boundary state, combine compatible states upward, and backtrack from the best root state to obtain an optimum.
knowledge_statements.title: Decomposition-Based Optimization

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The dynamic-programming pattern fits the optimization leaf, but no optimization problem, feasibility domain, objective, or rule-specific boundary semantics is fixed. A source or formal project specification is required to make the algorithm mathematically determinate.

children.title: Decomposition Tree Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Information passed between decomposition nodes, basic classes, and reconstructed instances.

assumptions_latex: Each permitted split maps a graph to an ordered finite list of blocks.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The rooted tree \(T(G)\), its split labels, marker maps, and boundary maps form the decomposition interface.

notation.meaning: The rooted decomposition tree of G
The graph block represented by node t
The interface data attached to an edge from t to a child u

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the data contract consumed by recognition and optimization routines.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A decomposition tree interface represents \(G\) by a rooted tree \(T(G)\). Its root \(r\) carries \(G_r=G\). Every internal node \(t\) carries a decomposition-rule label, a block \(G_t\), and children whose blocks are exactly those produced by that rule. Every edge \(tu\) carries a map \(\phi_{tu}\) identifying retained original vertices, markers, separator copies, and boundary states. Leaves carry basic graphs. The interface is valid when every internal record locally verifies its split and the rule-specific reconstruction map recovers feasible parent objects from compatible child objects.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A decomposition tree stores graph blocks, split types, markers, vertex maps, and boundary compatibility data needed to reconstruct parent solutions.
knowledge_statements.title: Decomposition Tree Interfaces

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation kind fits the leaf, but the marker, separator, boundary-state, and reconstruction maps are only named rather than formally typed. No source or project specification supports this proposed interface.

children.title: Algorithmic Failure Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Graph regimes where available decompositions do not directly support recognition or optimization.

assumptions_latex: A recursive graph procedure relies on decomposition into blocks and subsequent recombination.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Without bounded recursion, tractable leaves, and sufficient interface states, decomposition alone gives neither polynomial time nor correctness.

notation.meaning: Number of nodes in the produced decomposition tree

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A decomposition-based algorithm can fail in three independent ways. First, if recursion does not strictly decrease a well-founded size measure, it may not terminate. Second, if blocks are duplicated so that \(|T(G)|\) is superpolynomial, polynomial work per node does not imply polynomial total time. Third, if a basic leaf problem is intractable or the retained state set \(S_H\) omits information needed for compatibility, leaf tractability does not yield a correct global algorithm. Therefore termination, polynomial representation size, tractable leaves, and lossless recombination are separate obligations.

knowledge_statements.title: t-Perfect Graphs

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Weighted Min–Max Characterization of Strong t-Perfection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition of weighted vertex-edge-odd-circuit covers, their weak-duality bound, and the equality characterization of strong t-perfection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) and \(w:V\to\mathbb{Z}_{+}\). A \(w\)-cover is a family of vertices, edges, and odd circuits covering each vertex \(v\) at least \(w(v)\) times. A vertex or edge has cost \(1\), and an odd circuit \(C\) has cost \(\lfloor |V(C)|/2\rfloor\). Let \(\alpha_w(G)\) be the maximum weight of a stable set and \(\widetilde{\rho}_w(G)\) the minimum cost of a \(w\)-cover. Then \(\alpha_w(G)\le\widetilde{\rho}_w(G)\) for every graph, and \(G\) is strongly \(t\)-perfect if and only if \(\alpha_w(G)=\widetilde{\rho}_w(G)\) for every \(w:V\to\mathbb{Z}_{+}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For integral vertex weights, a w-cover consists of vertices, edges, and odd circuits covering each vertex to its required multiplicity, with costs 1, 1, and half the circuit length rounded down. Maximum stable-set weight is at most minimum w-cover cost, and equality for every such weight function characterizes strongly t-perfect graphs.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \alpha_w(G)\le\widetilde{\rho}_w(G),\qquad G\text{ is strongly }t\text{-perfect}\iff(\forall w:V\to\mathbb{Z}_{+})\ \alpha_w(G)=\widetilde{\rho}_w(G)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Polyhedral characterization of h-perfect graphs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines h-perfect graphs by exactness of the clique-and-odd-circuit relaxation and records the equivalent theta-body formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A graph \(G\) is h-perfect if and only if \(\operatorname{QSTAB}(G)\cap\operatorname{CSTAB}(G)=\operatorname{STAB}(G)\); equivalently, \(\operatorname{TH}(G)\cap\operatorname{CSTAB}(G)=\operatorname{STAB}(G)\). Thus nonnegativity, clique, and odd-circuit inequalities suffice to describe \(\operatorname{STAB}(G)\). Separately, if membership in both \(\mathcal L_1\operatorname{STAB}(G)\) and \(\mathcal L_2\operatorname{STAB}(G)\) is decidable in polynomial time, then membership in their intersection \((\mathcal L_1\cup\mathcal L_2)\operatorname{STAB}(G)\) is decidable in polynomial time.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A graph is h-perfect exactly when nonnegativity, clique, and odd-circuit inequalities describe its stable-set polytope; the source also gives the equivalent theta-body intersection characterization. Polynomial-time membership is preserved under intersecting two relaxation systems.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Lovász theta number
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Semidefinite definition of the Lovász theta number of a finite graph; the separately extracted sandwich and approximation results should carry its stated properties.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a finite graph \(G=(V,E)\), let \(\mathcal M_G\) be the set of symmetric matrices \(M\in\mathbb R^{V\times V}\) such that \(M_{uv}=0\) for every pair of distinct adjacent vertices \(u,v\), and \(\operatorname{Tr}M=1\). With \(\mathbf 1\in\mathbb R^V\) denoting the all-one vector, define
\[
\vartheta(G):=\max\left\{\mathbf 1^{\top}M\mathbf 1\mid M\in\mathcal M_G,\ M\succeq0\right\}.
\]

knowledge_statements.title: Orthonormal Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Handle formulation of the Lovász theta number.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An orthonormal representation of a finite simple graph \(G=(V,E)\) assigns a unit vector \(u_v\in\mathbb R^d\) to each \(v\in V\) so that \(u_v^{\mathsf T}u_w=0\) whenever distinct vertices \(v,w\) are nonadjacent. With a unit handle \(c\in\mathbb R^d\), the Lovász theta number has the representation \[\vartheta(G)=\min_{(u,c)}\ \max_{v\in V}\frac{1}{(c^{\mathsf T}u_v)^2},\] where the minimum ranges over all dimensions, such representations, and handles; a zero denominator is interpreted as \(+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Theta is the best worst-case inverse squared handle projection over orthonormal representations in which nonadjacent vertices receive orthogonal vectors.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\displaystyle \vartheta(G)=\min_{(u,c)}\max_{v\in V}(c^{\mathsf T}u_v)^{-2}.\)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Orthonormal representations and the graph theta body
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines graph orthonormal representations, their valid stable-set inequalities, the resulting theta body, and weighted optimization over that body. The OCR-ambiguous auxiliary quotient convention is excluded.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a graph $G=(V,E)$, an orthonormal representation is a family $(u_i)_{i\in V}$ in some $\mathbb R^N$, $N\ge 1$, such that $\|u_i\|=1$ for all $i\in V$ and $u_i^Tu_j=0$ whenever $i$ and $j$ are nonadjacent. If $c\in\mathbb R^N$ is a unit vector, then every stable set $S\subseteq V$ satisfies $\sum_{i\in S}(c^Tu_i)^2\le 1$. Consequently, $\sum_{i\in V}(c^Tu_i)^2x_i\le 1$ is valid for $\operatorname{STAB}(G)$. The set of nonnegative vectors satisfying all such inequalities is $\operatorname{TH}(G)$, and $\operatorname{STAB}(G)\subseteq\operatorname{TH}(G)\subseteq\operatorname{QSTAB}(G)$. For $w\in\mathbb R_+^V$, $\vartheta(G,w):=\max\{w^Tx:x\in\operatorname{TH}(G)\}$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An orthonormal representation assigns unit vectors to vertices so that nonadjacent vertices receive orthogonal vectors. Squared projections onto any unit vector yield valid stable-set inequalities. The nonnegative vectors satisfying all such inequalities form the theta body, which lies between the stable-set and fractional stable-set bodies. The weighted theta value is linear optimization over this body.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \sum_{i\in S}(c^Tu_i)^2\le1,\qquad \operatorname{STAB}(G)\subseteq\operatorname{TH}(G)\subseteq\operatorname{QSTAB}(G),\qquad \vartheta(G,w)=\max_{x\in\operatorname{TH}(G)}w^Tx

knowledge_statements.title: Semidefinite Theta Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Trace-normalized primal semidefinite formulation of theta.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite simple graph \(G=(V,E)\), let \(J\) be the all-ones matrix indexed by \(V\). The Lovász theta number admits the semidefinite representation \[\vartheta(G)=\max\left\{\langle J,X\rangle: X\in\mathbb S_+^V,\ \operatorname{Tr}(X)=1,\ X_{uv}=0\text{ for every }uv\in E\right\}.\] Here \(\langle A,B\rangle=\operatorname{Tr}(A^{\mathsf T}B)\). This normalization gives \(\vartheta(K_n)=1\) and \(\vartheta(\overline{K_n})=n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Theta equals an SDP maximizing the sum of matrix entries over positive semidefinite, trace-one matrices vanishing on graph edges.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\displaystyle \vartheta(G)=\max\{\langle J,X\rangle:X\succeq0,\operatorname{Tr}(X)=1,X_{uv}=0\ (uv\in E)\}.\)

notation.meaning: Cone of positive semidefinite symmetric matrices indexed by V.

review_flags: No supplied locator specifically supports this SDP normalization of theta.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The SDP representation fits the container and is internally coherent, but its edge-zero and trace-one normalization has no supporting citation or locator.

knowledge_statements.title: Theta Bodies
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lifted-semidefinite relaxation of the stable-set polytope.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite simple graph \(G=(V,E)\), its theta body is \[\operatorname{TH}(G)=\left\{x\in\mathbb R^V:\exists X\in\mathbb S^V,\ \begin{pmatrix}1&x^{\mathsf T}\\x&X\end{pmatrix}\succeq0,\ X_{vv}=x_v\ (v\in V),\ X_{uv}=0\ (uv\in E)\right\}.\] Every stable-set incidence vector has such a lift, and every point in the theta body satisfies all clique inequalities. Consequently, \[\operatorname{STAB}(G)\subseteq\operatorname{TH}(G)\subseteq\operatorname{QSTAB}(G).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The theta body is a semidefinite lift containing the stable-set polytope and contained in the fractional clique relaxation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{STAB}(G)\subseteq\operatorname{TH}(G)\subseteq\operatorname{QSTAB}(G).\)

notation.meaning: Nonnegative polyhedron satisfying every clique inequality.
Symmetric lifting matrix indexed by V.

review_flags: No supplied locator specifically supports this theta-body lift and normalization.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition kind and lifted formulation fit the theta-body container, but the exact lift and sandwich inclusions need a source with a specific locator.

knowledge_statements.title: Theta Stable-Set Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Primal theta witnesses derived from stable sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\) be a nonempty stable set of a finite simple graph \(G=(V,E)\), and let \(z=\mathbf1_S\). Then \[X_S=\frac{zz^{\mathsf T}}{|S|}\] is positive semidefinite, has trace one, and satisfies \((X_S)_{uv}=0\) for every edge \(uv\in E\). Its objective value in the trace-normalized theta SDP is \(\langle J,X_S\rangle=|S|\). Hence \(X_S\) is a directly verifiable certificate that \(\vartheta(G)\ge |S|\), and therefore \(\alpha(G)\le\vartheta(G)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A stable set yields a rank-one feasible theta matrix whose value is its cardinality, certifying a lower bound on theta.
assumptions_latex: \(S\subseteq V\) is a nonempty stable set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(X_S=\mathbf1_S\mathbf1_S^{\mathsf T}/|S|\implies \vartheta(G)\ge |S|.\)

notation.meaning: Rank-one theta SDP witness induced by S.

review_flags: No supplied locator specifically supports the theta stable-set certificate.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The rank-one witness is appropriately classified as a certificate and is consistent with the stated SDP, but no cited source supports this certificate formulation.

children.title: Theta Coloring Certificates

knowledge_statements.title: Theta Coloring Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Colorings provide complement-theta upper certificates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite simple graph with a proper coloring \(V=C_1\dot\cup\cdots\dot\cup C_k\). Each \(C_i\) is stable in \(G\), hence a clique in \(\overline G\). The clique inequalities of \(\operatorname{TH}(\overline G)\) give \[\sum_{v\in V}x_v=\sum_{i=1}^k\sum_{v\in C_i}x_v\le k\qquad(x\in\operatorname{TH}(\overline G)).\] Thus the displayed coloring is a verifiable certificate that \(\vartheta(\overline G)\le k\), yielding \(\vartheta(\overline G)\le\chi(G)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proper k-coloring partitions vertices into complement cliques and certifies that the complement's theta number is at most k.
assumptions_latex: \(C_1,\ldots,C_k\) are the color classes of a proper coloring.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(V=C_1\dot\cup\cdots\dot\cup C_k\implies\vartheta(\overline G)\le k.\)
review_flags: No supplied locator specifically supports the theta coloring certificate.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The coloring witness fits the certificate container and is internally consistent with the stated theta-body convention, but it lacks cited support.

children.title: Theta Clique-Cover Certificates

knowledge_statements.title: Theta Clique-Cover Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Clique covers provide theta upper certificates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite simple graph and suppose \(V=K_1\cup\cdots\cup K_k\), where every \(K_i\) is a clique. Assign each vertex to one containing clique to obtain a clique partition \(V=K'_1\dot\cup\cdots\dot\cup K'_k\), allowing empty parts. Since every \(x\in\operatorname{TH}(G)\) satisfies clique inequalities, \[\sum_{v\in V}x_v=\sum_{i=1}^k\sum_{v\in K'_i}x_v\le k.\] Therefore the cover certifies \(\vartheta(G)\le k\), and minimizing over covers gives \(\vartheta(G)\le\overline\chi(G)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cover by k cliques certifies that theta is at most k by summing the corresponding clique inequalities.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(V=K_1\cup\cdots\cup K_k\implies\vartheta(G)\le k.\)

notation.meaning: Minimum number of cliques covering V.

review_flags: No supplied locator specifically supports the theta clique-cover certificate.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The clique-cover argument fits the certificate container, but the theta upper-bound certificate and its dependence on clique inequalities are uncited.

children.title: Complement-Dual Certificate Transfer
children.top_down_role: Correspondence between coloring and clique-cover certificate viewpoints under graph complementation.

knowledge_statements.title: Complement-Dual Certificate Transfer
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Complementation exchanges coloring and clique-cover theta certificates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every finite simple graph \(G\), a subset of vertices is stable in \(G\) exactly when it is a clique in \(\overline G\). Consequently, a proper \(k\)-coloring of \(G\) is the same vertex partition as a \(k\)-clique cover of \(\overline G\), and it certifies \(\vartheta(\overline G)\le k\). Conversely, a \(k\)-clique cover of \(G\) transfers to a proper \(k\)-coloring of \(\overline G\) and certifies \(\vartheta(G)\le k\). Thus \[\chi(G)=\overline\chi(\overline G),\qquad \overline\chi(G)=\chi(\overline G).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Complementation turns color classes into cliques and clique covers into colorings, transferring the associated theta upper certificates.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\chi(G)=\overline\chi(\overline G)\text{ and }\overline\chi(G)=\chi(\overline G).\)
review_flags: No supplied locator specifically supports complement transfer for theta certificates.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The duality classification fits complement transfer, and the complement identities are coherent, but the associated theta-certificate transfer has no cited source.

children.title: Certificate Exactness Regimes

knowledge_statements.title: Certificate Exactness Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Matching stable-set and clique-cover certificates force theta exactness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite simple graph. If \(S\subseteq V\) is stable and \(K_1,\ldots,K_k\) are cliques covering \(V\), with \(|S|=k\), then the theta sandwich gives \[k=|S|\le\alpha(G)\le\vartheta(G)\le\overline\chi(G)\le k.\] Hence all displayed quantities equal \(k\); the stable set and clique cover jointly certify optimality and theta exactness. Dually, a clique of size \(k\) and a proper \(k\)-coloring certify \(\omega(G)=\vartheta(\overline G)=\chi(G)=k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Equal-sized stable-set and clique-cover witnesses force equality throughout the theta sandwich; the complementary clique-coloring condition gives the dual regime.
assumptions_latex: \(S\) is stable and \(K_1,\ldots,K_k\) cover V by cliques.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(|S|=k\implies\alpha(G)=\vartheta(G)=\overline\chi(G)=k.\)
review_flags: No supplied locator specifically supports the theta sandwich certificate regime.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The sufficient matching-witness condition fits the exactness-regime container, but the theta sandwich and complementary exactness assertion require cited support.

knowledge_statements.title: Theta Exactness on Perfect Graphs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unweighted theta exactness and theta-body equality for perfect graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite perfect graph. Then its theta body equals its stable-set polytope, \[\operatorname{TH}(G)=\operatorname{STAB}(G).\] Consequently, maximizing the all-ones objective yields \[\alpha(G)=\vartheta(G)=\overline\chi(G)=\chi(\overline G).\] Since the complement of a perfect graph is perfect, applying the same assertion to \(\overline G\) also gives \[\omega(G)=\vartheta(\overline G)=\chi(G).\] Thus the lower stable-set or clique certificates and the complementary coloring or clique-cover certificates are exact on perfect graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a perfect graph, the theta body is the stable-set polytope, so theta equals the stable-set and clique-cover optima, with complementary dual equalities.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{TH}(G)=\operatorname{STAB}(G)\text{ and }\alpha(G)=\vartheta(G)=\chi(\overline G).\)
review_flags: No supplied locator specifically supports theta-body exactness on perfect graphs.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem kind fits the exactness container, but theta-body equality for perfect graphs and the resulting equalities are substantial claims with no citation or inspectable locator.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Theta Characterizations of Perfect Graphs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent induced-subgraph characterizations through theta exactness and integrality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every graph \(G\), the following are equivalent: (i) \(G\) is perfect; (ii) \(\alpha(H)=\vartheta(H)\) for every induced subgraph \(H\) of \(G\); (iii) \(\vartheta(H)=\bar{\chi}^{*}(H)\) for every induced subgraph \(H\) of \(G\); (iv) \(\vartheta(H)\in\mathbb{Z}\) for every induced subgraph \(H\) of \(G\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A graph G is perfect if and only if every induced subgraph H satisfies alpha(H) = theta(H); equivalently, every such H satisfies theta(H) equal to its fractional clique-cover number; equivalently, theta(H) is an integer for every such H.
assumptions_latex: H\text{ ranges over all induced subgraphs of }G
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: G\text{ is perfect}\iff(\forall H\leq_{\mathrm{ind}}G)\,\alpha(H)=\vartheta(H)\iff(\forall H\leq_{\mathrm{ind}}G)\,\vartheta(H)=\bar{\chi}^{*}(H)\iff(\forall H\leq_{\mathrm{ind}}G)\,\vartheta(H)\in\mathbb{Z}

children.title: Weighted Theta Numbers
children.top_down_role: Weight-sensitive theta parameters, their graph-class scope, and optimization interpretation.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\alpha(G,w)\le \vartheta(G,w)\), with equality whenever \(\operatorname{TH}(G)=\operatorname{STAB}(G)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Theta-body formulation for nonnegative vertex weights.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(\operatorname{TH}(G)\) as the set of vectors \(x\in\mathbb{R}^{V}\) for which there exists \(X\in\mathbb{S}^{V}\) satisfying \[\begin{pmatrix}1&x^{\mathsf T}\\x&X\end{pmatrix}\succeq0,\qquad X_{ii}=x_i\ \text{for all }i\in V,\qquad X_{ij}=0\ \text{for all }ij\in E.\] The weighted theta number is \[\vartheta(G,w):=\max\{w^{\mathsf T}x:x\in\operatorname{TH}(G)\}.\] Since every incidence vector of a stable set belongs to \(\operatorname{TH}(G)\), the weighted stability number \(\alpha(G,w):=\max\{w(S):S\subseteq V\text{ stable}\}\) satisfies \(\alpha(G,w)\le\vartheta(G,w)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The weighted theta number maximizes the vertex-weight objective over the theta body, giving a semidefinite upper bound on maximum-weight stable sets.
knowledge_statements.title: Weighted Theta Numbers

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The weighted theta-body definition and bound are mathematically coherent, and the definition kind fits the leaf. No cited source or inspectable locator supports the SDP convention or exactness claim; the explanatory derivation should also be removed from the eventual statement.

children.title: Strengthened Theta Numbers
children.top_down_role: Tighter theta-type parameters obtained through enhanced relaxation families.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\alpha(G,w)\le \vartheta'(G,w)\le \vartheta(G,w)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the Schrijver nonnegative-matrix strengthening.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The strengthened weighted theta number in the Schrijver convention is \[\vartheta'(G,w):=\max\left\{w^{\mathsf T}x:\begin{pmatrix}1&x^{\mathsf T}\\x&X\end{pmatrix}\succeq0,\ X_{ii}=x_i\ (i\in V),\ X_{ij}=0\ (ij\in E),\ X_{ij}\ge0\ (i,j\in V)\right\}.\] The added entrywise-nonnegativity constraints preserve every stable-set incidence solution and restrict the feasible region of the ordinary theta relaxation. Consequently, \(\alpha(G,w)\le\vartheta'(G,w)\le\vartheta(G,w)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Schrijver's strengthened theta number adds entrywise nonnegativity to the theta semidefinite program, tightening the weighted stable-set upper bound.
knowledge_statements.title: Strengthened Theta Numbers

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the strengthened-theta leaf, but theta-prime conventions vary. An authoritative source must specifically support this entrywise-nonnegative SDP and the stated weighted dominance chain.

children.title: Variant Dominance Regimes
children.top_down_role: Relative strength, coincidence cases, and separation boundaries among theta variants.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\alpha(G,w)\le\vartheta'(G,w)\le\vartheta(G,w)\), with equality throughout when \(G\) is perfect.

notation.meaning: strengthened and ordinary weighted theta numbers

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dominance for Schrijver's strengthening and perfect-graph collapse.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every finite simple graph \(G\) and nonnegative weight vector \(w\), feasibility of stable-set incidence vectors and nesting of the semidefinite feasible regions give \[\alpha(G,w)\le\vartheta'(G,w)\le\vartheta(G,w).\] If \(G\) is perfect, its theta body equals its stable-set polytope, so both relaxations have the same support function as \(\operatorname{STAB}(G)\). Hence \[\alpha(G,w)=\vartheta'(G,w)=\vartheta(G,w).\] Outside this exactness regime either inequality may be strict, so the strengthened value can distinguish a tighter relaxation from the ordinary theta value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The strengthened theta value lies between weighted stability and ordinary theta; all three coincide on perfect graphs.
knowledge_statements.title: Variant Dominance Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property kind and dominance statement fit the container. Sources are required for the selected theta-prime convention and for the perfect-graph collapse of both weighted relaxations.

children.title: Weighted Exactness Regimes
children.top_down_role: Graph classes and weight settings where weighted theta parameters are exact.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(G\) is perfect, then \(\vartheta(G,w)=\vartheta'(G,w)=\alpha(G,w)\) for every \(w\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weighted exactness characterized through equality of convex bodies.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite simple graph \(G\), the following are equivalent: \(G\) is perfect; \(\operatorname{TH}(G)=\operatorname{STAB}(G)\); and \[\vartheta(G,w)=\alpha(G,w)\qquad\text{for every }w\in\mathbb{R}_{\ge0}^{V}.\] Under these conditions the Schrijver-strengthened body lies between the stable-set polytope and the ordinary theta body, and therefore \[\vartheta'(G,w)=\vartheta(G,w)=\alpha(G,w)\qquad\text{for every }w\in\mathbb{R}_{\ge0}^{V}.\] Thus perfect graphs form a weight-uniform exactness regime, rather than one depending on a particular objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A graph is perfect exactly when weighted theta equals weighted stability for every nonnegative weight vector; the strengthened variant is then exact too.
knowledge_statements.title: Weighted Exactness Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem kind fits the exactness-regime leaf, and the weight-uniform characterization is plausible under the stated theta-body convention. No source or locator supports the equivalence and strengthened-variant conclusion.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strong Graph Product and Shannon Capacity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the strong graph powers used in the asymptotic independence-number definition of Shannon capacity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For graphs \(G\) and \(H\), the strong product \(G\cdot H\) has vertex set \(V(G)\times V(H)\). Distinct vertices \((u,v)\) and \((u',v')\) are adjacent if and only if \((u=u'\text{ or }uu'\in E(G))\) and \((v=v'\text{ or }vv'\in E(H))\). If \(G^k\) denotes the strong product of \(k\) copies of \(G\), then \(\Theta(G)=\sup_{k\geq1}\alpha(G^k)^{1/k}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The strong product of G and H has ordered-pair vertices; two distinct pairs are adjacent exactly when each pair of corresponding coordinates is equal or adjacent in its factor. The Shannon capacity of G is the supremum over positive integers k of the kth root of the independence number of the kth strong power of G.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: V(G\cdot H)=V(G)\times V(H),\qquad \Theta(G)=\sup_{k\geq1}\sqrt[k]{\alpha(G^k)}

children.title: Theta under Graph Products
children.top_down_role: Behavior of theta parameters across standard graph-product constructions.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\vartheta(G\boxtimes H)=\vartheta(G)\vartheta(H)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Multiplicativity for the strong product used in zero-error capacity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\boxtimes H\) be the graph on \(V(G)\times V(H)\) in which distinct \((g,h)\) and \((g',h')\) are adjacent exactly when each coordinate is equal or adjacent in its factor and at least one coordinate is adjacent. The Lovász theta number is multiplicative under this product: \[\vartheta(G\boxtimes H)=\vartheta(G)\vartheta(H).\] Consequently, for every integer \(n\ge1\), \[\vartheta(G^{\boxtimes n})=\vartheta(G)^n.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Lovász theta is multiplicative under the strong graph product, and therefore multiplicative over every strong power.
knowledge_statements.title: Theta under Graph Products

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem kind fits the leaf and the strong-product convention is explicitly stated. Multiplicativity is a nontrivial theorem requiring an authoritative theorem or section locator.

children.title: Graph-Product Regimes
children.top_down_role: Product types relevant to theta analysis and zero-error information settings.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Strong products model confusability composition, while disjunctive products are obtained by complementation.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Product conventions relevant to theta and zero-error capacity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The strong product \(G\boxtimes H\) has vertex set \(V(G)\times V(H)\), with distinct \((g,h)\) and \((g',h')\) adjacent when \((g=g'\text{ or }gg'\in E(G))\) and \((h=h'\text{ or }hh'\in E(H))\). The disjunctive product \(G*H\) joins them when \(gg'\in E(G)\) or \(hh'\in E(H)\). These conventions satisfy \[\overline{G\boxtimes H}=\overline G*\overline H.\] Strong powers govern the independent-set formulation of Shannon capacity; complementary disjunctive powers give the equivalent clique formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strong products compose confusability graphs; disjunctive products give the complementary clique formulation, with the two regimes linked by graph complementation.
knowledge_statements.title: Graph-Product Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition kind fits the product-regime leaf, but the product terminology, complementation identity, and operational interpretations require a source with a specific locator.

children.title: Theta Bounds for Shannon Capacity
children.top_down_role: The role of theta parameters as bounds in Shannon-capacity analysis.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Theta(G)\le\vartheta(G)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Confusability-graph convention for Shannon capacity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define the Shannon capacity of a finite confusability graph \(G\) by \[\Theta(G):=\sup_{n\ge1}\alpha(G^{\boxtimes n})^{1/n}.\] For every \(n\ge1\), the stable-set bound and theta multiplicativity give \[\alpha(G^{\boxtimes n})\le\vartheta(G^{\boxtimes n})=\vartheta(G)^n.\] Taking \(n\)-th roots and the supremum yields \[\alpha(G)\le\Theta(G)\le\vartheta(G).\] Thus a single semidefinite theta computation bounds independent-message growth over all block lengths.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Shannon capacity is the asymptotic independent-set growth rate of strong graph powers and is at most the Lovász theta number.
knowledge_statements.title: Theta Bounds for Shannon Capacity

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem kind fits the capacity-bound leaf, and the confusability-graph convention is stated consistently. The capacity definition, theta multiplicativity, and resulting bound need authoritative citations.

children.title: Capacity Exactness Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Graph families exhibiting exactness, strict gaps, or unresolved capacity behavior.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Theta(G)=\vartheta(G)\) exactly when strong powers asymptotically attain the theta bound.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exactness criterion plus standard sufficient regimes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Theta is exact for the Shannon capacity of \(G\) precisely when \[\sup_{n\ge1}\alpha(G^{\boxtimes n})^{1/n}=\vartheta(G),\] equivalently, when for every \(\varepsilon>0\) some \(n\ge1\) satisfies \[\alpha(G^{\boxtimes n})\ge\bigl(\vartheta(G)-\varepsilon\bigr)^n.\] A sufficient finite-power certificate is \(\alpha(G^{\boxtimes n})=\vartheta(G)^n\) for some \(n\). In particular, \(\alpha(G)=\vartheta(G)\) implies exactness already at \(n=1\), whereas a uniform exponential gap below \(\vartheta(G)^n\) certifies failure of theta exactness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Theta equals Shannon capacity exactly when independent sets in strong powers asymptotically attain theta's multiplicative bound; equality at one power is sufficient.
knowledge_statements.title: Capacity Exactness Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The exactness condition and finite-power sufficient certificate fit the leaf. The final phrase about a uniform exponential gap is not quantitatively defined, and no source supports the characterization or boundary claims.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural recognition criterion from the Strong Perfect Graph Theorem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A finite simple graph \(G\) is perfect if and only if neither \(G\) nor its complement contains an induced odd cycle of length at least five. Equivalently, \(G\) is perfect exactly when it contains no odd hole and no odd antihole. This characterization yields verifiable obstruction certificates for nonperfection. Moreover, perfect-graph recognition is solvable in polynomial time: a recognition algorithm either declares \(G\) perfect or returns an induced odd hole or odd antihole witnessing that it is not perfect.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A graph is perfect exactly when it has no induced odd hole or odd antihole; polynomial recognition can return such an obstruction.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A maximum-weight clique of \(G\) is computable in time polynomial in \(|V|\) and the encoding length of \(w\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a perfect graph \(G=(V,E)\) and rational vertex weights \(w\). Form the complement \(\overline G\), which is perfect. Recover an optimal incidence vector by standard optimization-to-solution reconstruction and output its support. Because stable sets of \(\overline G\) are cliques of \(G\), the output is a maximum-weight clique of \(G\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polynomial-time exact optimization on a perfect graph after removing negative-weight vertices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a finite perfect graph \(G=(V,E)\) and binary-encoded rational weights \(w\in\mathbb{Q}^{V}\), let \(U:=\{v\in V:w_v\ge 0\}\). Compute a maximum-weight stable set of the perfect induced subgraph \(G[U]\) by exact polynomial-time optimization over \(\operatorname{TH}(G[U])=\operatorname{STAB}(G[U])\), reconstruct an optimal incidence vector, and return its support. Because no optimal stable set needs a negative-weight vertex, the returned set is maximum-weight for the original instance \((G,w)\).

children.title: Complementation Transfer
children.top_down_role: Transfer between weighted clique and weighted stable-set viewpoints through graph complementation.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\omega(G,w)=\alpha(\overline G,w)\), and perfectness is preserved by complementation.

notation.meaning: maximum weight of a stable set

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Objective-preserving transfer between clique and stable-set optimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every subset \(S\subseteq V\), \(S\) is a clique of \(G\) if and only if \(S\) is a stable set of \(\overline G\). Therefore the identity map on vertex subsets preserves weights and gives \[\omega(G,w):=\max_{S\text{ clique in }G}\sum_{v\in S}w_v=\max_{S\text{ stable in }\overline G}\sum_{v\in S}w_v=\alpha(\overline G,w).\] Likewise, \(\alpha(G,w)=\omega(\overline G,w)\). Since \(G\) is perfect if and only if \(\overline G\) is perfect, polynomial-time weighted optimization transfers in both directions within the perfect-graph class.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cliques of a graph are exactly stable sets of its complement, preserving weights, optimum values, and membership in the perfect-graph class.
knowledge_statements.title: Complementation Transfer

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The duality kind fits the complementation-transfer leaf, and the weighted clique–stable-set identities are consistent when the empty set is allowed. The preservation of perfectness under complementation and the optimization-transfer claim require authoritative citations.

knowledge_statements.title: Weight-Regime Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates integral multicoloring demands from rational fractional weights and invalid negative demands.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite perfect graph. For every demand vector \(w\in\mathbb Z_{\ge 0}^{V}\), the integral weighted coloring identity is \[\min\left\{\sum_{S\in\mathcal S(G)}y_S:y\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^{\mathcal S(G)},\ \sum_{S\ni v}y_S\ge w_v\ (v\in V)\right\}=\max_{K\in\mathcal K(G)}\sum_{v\in K}w_v.\] This formulation does not extend literally to nonintegral demands because its left side is integer-valued. Replacing \(y\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^{\mathcal S(G)}\) by \(y\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}^{\mathcal S(G)}\) defines fractional weighted coloring instead. Negative coordinates are outside the demand interpretation and make the displayed covering model inappropriate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The integral clique–coloring identity uses nonnegative integer demands. Rational or real demands require fractional coloring, while negative weights are not valid coloring demands.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal S(G)\) and \(\mathcal K(G)\) contain all stable sets and cliques, including the empty set.
The integral identity is asserted only for \(w\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^{V}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\chi(G,w)=\omega(G,w)\) in the integral nonnegative regime; nonintegral and negative weights require different formulations.

notation.meaning: family of stable sets of G
integral coloring demand at vertex v

review_flags: Exact weighted perfect-graph theorem locator is absent from the supplied inventory hints.
The fractional and negative-weight boundary requires source confirmation.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The integral identity and the asserted boundaries for fractional and negative demands are mathematically plausible and fit the failure-boundary leaf, but no citation supports them. A specific theorem or section locator addressing weighted coloring and these regime distinctions is required.

knowledge_statements.title: Weighted Coloring on Perfect Graphs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Integral vertex-demand form of the weighted perfect-graph theorem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite perfect graph and let \(w\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^{V}\). Assign a nonnegative integer multiplicity \(y_S\) to every stable set \(S\) so that each vertex \(v\) is covered at least \(w_v\) times. Then \[\chi(G,w):=\min\left\{\sum_{S\in\mathcal S(G)}y_S:y\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^{\mathcal S(G)},\ \sum_{S\ni v}y_S\ge w_v\ (v\in V)\right\}=\max_{K\in\mathcal K(G)}\sum_{v\in K}w_v=: \omega(G,w).\] Thus a maximum-weight clique is the exact dual obstruction to an integral weighted coloring of a perfect graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For nonnegative integer vertex demands on a perfect graph, the minimum number of stable-set color classes equals the maximum total demand of a clique.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\chi(G,w)=\omega(G,w)\).

notation.meaning: minimum number of stable-set color classes satisfying demands w
maximum total vertex demand over a clique
multiplicity assigned to stable set S

knowledge_statements.title: Strongly Polynomial Perfect-Graph Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Complexity criterion distinguishing strong polynomiality from bit-length-dependent perfect-graph optimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a family of finite perfect-graph instances \((G,w)\), an exact optimization algorithm is strongly polynomial when the number of arithmetic operations and comparisons is bounded by a polynomial in \(|V(G)|+|E(G)|\), independently of the magnitudes and encoding lengths of \(w\), and every intermediate rational number has encoding length polynomially bounded by the input length. Consequently, a runtime polynomial in \(|V(G)|+|E(G)|+\langle w\rangle\), or an iteration bound depending on \(\log\|w\|_\infty\), establishes only ordinary polynomiality unless an additional magnitude-independent bound is proved.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strong polynomiality requires an operation bound depending only on graph size, not weight bit length; bit-length- or magnitude-dependent bounds are merely polynomial.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite perfect graph supplied in an explicitly represented graph model.
\(w\) is rational input data with finite binary encoding length \(\langle w\rangle\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Strong polynomiality requires a polynomial bound in \(|V|+|E|\) independent of \(\langle w\rangle\) and \(\|w\|_\infty\).

notation.meaning: binary encoding length of the weight vector
